title_en: YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
title_fa: YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
excerpt_en: YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google. At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike...
excerpt_fa: YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google. At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike...
content_en:
YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google. At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike button being absent for them.
YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
Some users have reported that their YouTube dislike button has been moved to the three-dots menu.
Some users have reported that their YouTube dislike button has been moved to the three-dots menu.
Right now, for me, the dislike button sits right next to the like button under a video. Moving it to a submenu would make it considerably more of an effort to access, meaning that fewer people would likely use it.
It’s unclear how widely this apparent test may be rolled out, and Google didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
YouTube has shown a willingness to make changes to the dislike button. In 2021, it hid the public dislike count on videos to help “protect creators from harassment,” though creators can still see dislike counts. Earlier this year, YouTube removed the dislike button from YouTube Shorts, suggesting instead that users take advantage of options in the three-dots menu.

title_en: How much power can a 1kW wind turbine produce for your home?
title_fa: How much power can a 1kW wind turbine produce for your home?
excerpt_en: A 1 kW wind turbine can help with your electric bill, but the wind determines how much.
excerpt_fa: A 1 kW wind turbine can help with your electric bill, but the wind determines how much.
content_en:
How much power can a 1kW wind turbine produce for your home?
It all depends on the wind.
Do home wind turbines actually work? The answer is a very reserved "yes." With solar energy cruising into record territory, small-scale wind power for residential use tends to get lost in the sun (poor pun intended).There are several caveats, though wind power is not an altogether losing proposition. It really depends on the need and the scale of use. They even make compact turbines for powering RVs, so it also depends on your definition of "home."
It's important to note that a 1 kW turbine is a "peak" power measure, not necessarily what you'll get out of it. The more useful number to look at is annual or monthly energy production, measured in kilowatt-hours. In a carefully chosen position, a 1 kW turbine could feasibly produce 200 kWh per month, or about 2,400 kWh per year. That works out to under a quarter of the average US household's annual energy consumption.
None of this is to say that wind turbines are weak power producers — it just depends on the wind. If you live in an area with annual wind speeds averaging 14+ mph, this is something worth looking into. If not, or if windy days are sparse or even average, maybe not so much. A 1 kW system is feasible, but it's best to look at it in terms of supplemental power for an already efficient home.
Placement determines whether it works
A wind turbine for a home practically requires a high average wind speed that's consistent month-to-month. Homes with lots of trees, surrounded by other homes, behind hills or with large sheds need not apply. Not only do these obstacles block wind, but they also create turbulence, which reduces output and speeds up wear and tear on the turbine. The Department of Energy's small wind guidance recommends placing the bottom of the rotor at least 30 feet above any obstacle within 300 horizontal feet of the tower.
That recommendation alone tells you all you need to know about placing a wind turbine in a suburban neighborhood. It'll make for some interesting conversations at the neighbor's house, and little more. Worse, most local zoning rules limit structures to around 35 feet, and wind turbines often require much more in order to clear nearby trees and rooftops. A rooftop installation option sounds great on paper, but it can transmit vibration and noise directly into your rooftop, a lovely side effect while trying to catch some Zs before work.
If you're sold on wind power, look beyond your region's wind map, check local zoning and utility rules and conduct a thorough assessment of your site's obstacles and average wind direction. It's also a good idea to get an installer to estimate overall production before spending your hard-earned dough.
A whole-house turbine needs much more capacity
If your home is a small, economical little cabin or a permanently parked RV, a 1kW wind turbine is certainly an option. However, it's not enough to power a typical US home. The average household uses about 10,500 kWh of electricity per year (around 850 kWh per month), and a residential turbine in the 5 kW to 15 kW range is necessary to put a dent in that power consumption.
Cost is another reason to proceed with a bit of caution. It'll run the average consumer between $20,000 and $50,000 to toss up a wind turbine. Installing solar panels with the same energy production in mind is roughly $2,500 to $3,500, and that's before incentives are calculated in.
A grid-connected system typically requires an inverter as well and can offset some utility use when the wind is blowing. Off-grid systems will require batteries and a charge controller to store power. For the majority of suburban dwellers, improving insulation and tossing in some ground- or roof-mounted solar panels will provide more dependable, solid results. If you want to go the wind route, it makes the most sense in open, rural areas that have verified average wind speeds and a place to put your tower.

title_en: What can you use your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button for?
title_fa: What can you use your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button for?
excerpt_en: Here's what your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button can really do, from launching workouts and retracing routes to controlling smart home devices with one tap.
excerpt_fa: Here's what your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button can really do, from launching workouts and retracing routes to controlling smart home devices with one tap.
content_en:
What can you use your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button for?
That little orange button can do a lot more than start your next workout.
If you're serious about running, hiking, weightlifting or other high-energy activities, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is easy to recommend. At $800, it is a commitment — but that's surprisingly reasonable compared to other fitness and adventure watches, and the benefits over a regular Apple Watch aren't trivial. It's bigger, tougher and lasts up to 50 hours on a charge, whereas a Series 12 has to be topped up every day. Combined with its satellite features and GPS accuracy, it might legitimately save your life on a wilderness trek.
An Ultra difference that Apple tends to downplay these days is the action button. It's an orange button next to the speaker grille, used as a quick shortcut for commands that other Watch owners have to tap through menus or complications to reach. It can also activate the watch's emergency siren, which helps attract attention if you're lost or injured. It's such an obvious, low-cost feature that it's almost insulting that it's not on Series devices, too.
There's a broad range of commands you can assign to the button. You can only assign one at a time, but if you know what you're doing, it can be immensely useful for anything that's a daily habit. All the more so if you take advantage of the automation upgrades in watchOS 27 and iOS 27.
The action button arsenal on your wrist
If you hold down the action button briefly, you'll see the Quick Switch menu appear. This lets you swap the button's single-tap function on the fly, which can be vital for some activities, particularly outdoor navigation. You'll see what we mean in a moment.
The most straightforward options are Flashlight, Voice Memo, Translate and Recognize Music. With these, you just hit the button once to start the function and again to stop it. As a side note, Recognize Music should be nearly instant on an Ultra 4, thanks to Apple's new Audio Intelligence capabilities, which also support automatic Shazam detection.
Slightly more complex are Workout, Stopwatch and Dive. With Stopwatch, pressing the button once starts timing, and pressing it again marks a lap. Press the action and side buttons simultaneously to pause. With Dive, a regular press begins your aquatic adventures, while pressing action and side simultaneously launches an app-specific secondary function.
Similarly, Workout will either open the Workout app or immediately launch into a particular activity. You can change this by going to Settings > Action Button. Mid-session, tapping the button performs a secondary function, such as marking a segment. To pause, press action and side together.
Special attention is due to the two navigation options, Waypoint and Backtrack. The first drops waypoints visible in the Compass app and the Waypoint watchface, although some waypoints are added automatically, such as your parked car and the last available cell signal. Backtrack is also linked to the Compass app, but tapping once starts recording a precise route you can retrace later. Hitting the action and side buttons simultaneously flips between the Record and Retrace modes.
The showstoppers: Accessibility and Shortcuts
For some users, assigning the button to Accessibility might be unavoidable. This lets you trigger things like AssistiveTouch, VoiceOver and even control nearby devices. There may be a reason to use this if you're fully able-bodied, too, so check it out.
Arguably, though, the single most powerful action is Shortcut. This is configured like Accessibility, but lets you trigger any automation you've built in the iPhone's Shortcuts app. Given that these automations can stretch across multiple platforms and even control smart home accessories, there's virtually unlimited potential. A single tap might, for example, turn on your lights, adjust your thermostat and even start playing local news on your HomePod.
The Shortcuts app can be unwieldy at times. Thankfully, a big change in iOS 27 on iPhones with Apple Intelligence is the ability to build shortcuts simply by describing what you want them to do. This greatly simplifies the process, although it's important to double-check the results. You don't want an "I'm driving home" routine to accidentally send an ETA to your mother-in-law instead of your partner.

title_en: Judge dismisses Sam Altman’s sister’s sexual abuse lawsuit
title_fa: Judge dismisses Sam Altman’s sister’s sexual abuse lawsuit
excerpt_en: On Tuesday, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the lawsuit Ann Altman filed last year alleging that her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, had sexually abused her throughout her childhood. As reported earlier by The Guardian, the judge wrote that over the past year, Ann...
excerpt_fa: On Tuesday, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the lawsuit Ann Altman filed last year alleging that her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, had sexually abused her throughout her childhood. As reported earlier by The Guardian, the judge wrote that over the past year, Ann...
content_en:
On Tuesday, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the lawsuit Ann Altman filed last year alleging that her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, had sexually abused her throughout her childhood. As reported earlier by The Guardian, the judge wrote that over the past year, Ann had failed to appear for an independent medical examination or meet other deadlines despite warnings that it would result in the case being dismissed.
Judge dismisses Sam Altman’s sister’s sexual abuse lawsuit
Ann Altman’s lawsuit against her brother was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled.
Ann Altman’s lawsuit against her brother was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled.
When the case was filed last year, a statement shared by Sam Altman, his mother, and his brothers said, “Annie has made deeply hurtful and entirely untrue claims about our family, and especially Sam… All of these claims are utterly untrue. This situation causes immense pain to our entire family.”
Bluestone granted Sam Altman’s motion to dismiss the case with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled in that court, while denying Sam’s request for attorney fees and costs. Santos Perez, a lawyer who had represented Ann until withdrawing this month, told The Guardian in a statement that “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”

title_en: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
title_fa: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
excerpt_en: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI running amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
excerpt_fa: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI running amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
content_en:
Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.
Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.
Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.
The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”
Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.
It’s not clear how this proposed system would ensure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).
In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a Washington, D.C., judge a halt to the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.
The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.
In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.
Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers who are placed inside AI organizations to monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.
Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, whose CEO, Jensen Huang, recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

title_en: Oura Ring can track new stats related to cardio fitness
title_fa: Oura Ring can track new stats related to cardio fitness
excerpt_en: Oura has updated its smart rings with new cardio fitness-related metrics, including VO2 Max estimates.
excerpt_fa: Oura has updated its smart rings with new cardio fitness-related metrics, including VO2 Max estimates.
content_en:
Oura Ring can track new stats related to cardio fitness
The smart rings are getting Cardio Effort and VO2 Max data.
Smart ring company Oura announced that it is adding two new fitness features. First is Cardio Effort, an assessment of how much strain the wearer has put on their body during activity. The personalized metric will offer five ranges — light, fair, maintaining, building and reaching — that offer a gauge of how the week's activities compare to the individual's baseline. The feature is based on the Training Impulse method and is designed to monitor long-term trends in cardiovascular activity, the company said.
The second feature is that the smart rings will automatically estimate VO2 Max stats. This feature was previously called Cardio Capacity in the Oura Labs tool. It wasn't an automatic metric and it required a six-minute walking test before it could be enabled. The revised VO2 Max makes passive estimations on regular GPS-enabled workouts, meaning the test is no longer needed. VO2 Max stats will be available in Oura Labs for the third-generation Oura Ring and later models.
These new additions further expand Oura's offerings for holistic health data. Other wearables, including the Apple Watch and Fitbit, have been able to track similar cardio metrics for some time, so the change could make Oura a viable option for people who prefer the ring form factor to the watch or bracelet ones.

title_en: Five things you should know before buying the iPhone Duo
title_fa: Five things you should know before buying the iPhone Duo
excerpt_en: From software limitations to the pre-sale deals, here's what you need to know ahead of the iPhone Duo launch.
excerpt_fa: From software limitations to the pre-sale deals, here's what you need to know ahead of the iPhone Duo launch.
content_en:
Five things you should know before buying the iPhone Duo
From software limitations to the pre-sale deals, here's what you need to know ahead of the iPhone Duo launch.
Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo begin this Friday, and the first units will be shipped to buyers on October 23. And there's a lot of hype around the Duo, since it's the first foldable iPhone ever — and represents the most radical change to the iPhone in a while. It's also the most expensive iPhone yet, starting at $1,999. Despite the price, the device comes with some trade-offs that we've already covered in detail. It lacks some popular features and the cameras aren't the best on an iPhone. Even so, many people are eager to buy one.
But before you go ahead with your pre-order on Friday, it's worth going over all these limitations and deciding whether the iPhone Duo is really for you. What you give up compared to a regular iPhone
Yes, the iPhone Duo is the most expensive iPhone in the lineup today — but that doesn't mean it has the best hardware in every respect. As we've previously covered, one of its biggest drawbacks is its cameras. Like midrange iPhones, the Duo has two rear cameras and no dedicated telephoto lens. You can still get a 2x "optical-quality" zoom thanks to a digital crop of the main 48-megapixel sensor, but it's nowhere near the quality of the zoom lens found on the iPhone 18 Pro. The front-facing camera also has a lower resolution compared to the latest iPhones, with only 12 megapixels instead of 18 megapixels. There's no variable aperture on the main lens either — that feature remains exclusive to the iPhone 18 Pro models.

The Action Button is gone, too, so you'll be limited to silencing your phone or accessing quick controls through the Control Center. Camera Control is still there, though, so you can still quickly open your favorite camera app with just a click.
Then there's the issue of apps. Apple has optimized iOS 27 to take advantage of the new foldable form factor, and apps can do the same. This means that menus and apps can automatically snap to fit two halves of the screen when you bend the hinge, for instance. However, when it comes to third-party apps, developers will have to update them so they, too, fill the entire screen of the iPhone Duo. Some popular apps, such as Netflix, Zoom and Slack, will already have updates available for the iPhone Duo on launch day, but most developers still have work to do. It's hard not to compare the iPhone Duo to other foldable phones on the market, especially since there are so many of them out there. Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold also starts at $1,899 and includes a telephoto lens with 5x optical zoom, which, according to our review, makes it one of the best camera systems on a foldable phone.
These comparisons are academic, of course. When it comes to getting one for yourself, you should think about the ecosystem. If you're already locked into the Apple ecosystem, the iPhone Duo is a strong choice. But if you're open to trying something different, it's definitely worth checking out the competition, too. Our comparisons of the Duo versus the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Duo versus the Pixel 11 Pro Fold go further into the details.

Carriers and Apple itself are already offering some deals for those who want to pre-order the iPhone Duo this Friday. Apple's trade-in program alone offers up to $885 off, depending on the phone you trade in, which helps offset the full price. Or you can pay in installments with your Apple Card, interest-free, with prices starting at $83.29 per month for 24 months on the base model. There's also Apple Upgrade, a financing program in partnership with Klarna, with prices starting at $57.99 per month for 24 months. At the end of the contract, you can either return the device, pay off the remaining balance or upgrade to a new iPhone.
Carriers are also going big on deals for the iPhone Duo, with AT&T offering up to $1,200 in trade-in credit for eligible devices. T-Mobile, on the other hand, offers up to $1,000 in trade-in credit for Xfinity Mobile Plus customers. Even if you don't trade in your old phone, Mobile Plus customers can get a $400 discount when pre-ordering an iPhone Duo. With prices exceeding $2,000, any discount is more than welcome.

Apple has introduced its own range of new accessories designed specifically for its first foldable phone, and you prefer a first-party option. It's only available in two colors, though: Navy Blue and Sand, to match the blue and silver iPhones.

title_en: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger
title_fa: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger
excerpt_en: Elon Musk likes the idea but says he is not on either committee, which is made up of independent directors.
excerpt_fa: Elon Musk likes the idea but says he is not on either committee, which is made up of independent directors.
content_en:
The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies.
“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees, so it’s this sort of a … It’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation,” Musk said in response to a question during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call.
Musk didn’t name the members of these special committees, only noting that they were independent directors. Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm; Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair; former Tesla CTO JB Straubel; Joe Gebbia; Jack Hartung; James Murdoch; and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing.
Neither Musk nor his brother Kimbal Musk is independent. Denholm, Gebbia, Ehrenpreis, Hartung, Murdoch, and Wilson-Thompson sit on a variety of established committees overseeing audit, compensation, and corporate governance.
SpaceX lists six independent directors, including Ehrenpreis, who is also the chair of the company’s compensation and nominating committee. Randy Glein, Donald Harrison, Steve Jurvetson, Luke Nosek, and Roelof Botha are also considered independent directors.
Antonio Gracias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent. Gracias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX. Gracias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements.
Musk said he supports the idea of the merger but cautioned that it is not a guaranteed outcome.
“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla Motor is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said, adding that he thinks it would be a good idea. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.”
The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transactions, he said.
The SpaceX IPO cemented Musk’s grip on the company — he has more than 50% voting power — which would make it easier to garner support for a merger from SpaceX shareholders. It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said, adding there was a lot to be gaining from cooperating on developing AI software, robotics, SpaceX’s orbital AI data center project Starmind, and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing project between Tesla and SpaceX.

title_en: Fitbit Edge vs. Fitbit Inspire 3: How these Google fitness trackers compare
title_fa: Fitbit Edge vs. Fitbit Inspire 3: How these Google fitness trackers compare
excerpt_en: Google's latest tracker is a middle ground between a simple tracker and full smartwatch.
excerpt_fa: Google's latest tracker is a middle ground between a simple tracker and full smartwatch.
content_en:
Fitbit Edge vs. Fitbit Inspire 3: How these Google fitness trackers compare
Google's latest tracker is a middle ground between a simple tracker and full smartwatch.
Google has unveiled the Fitbit Edge, its latest smartwatch for tracking your health, sleep and fitness. But with an aluminum case, a larger screen and a $180 price tag, is the upgrade worth it compared to the $99.95 Fitbit Inspire 3?
Bigger screen, premium aluminum case
Both the Fitbit Edge and the Fitbit Inspire 3 use an AMOLED display, but the Edge offers a screen that's 6.9mm (0.27in) wider than the Inspire 3. Otherwise, their dimensions are very similar, with the Edge coming in at 39.2 x 25.5 x 11.5mm compared to the Inspire 3's 39.32 x 18.6 x 11.75mm size.
The Fitbit Edge's 100 percent recycled aluminum case and more tactile side button could be another value-add for those looking for something that looks a little less like an athletic watch and more like something you could wear to work. By comparison, the Fitbit Inspire 3 is more rectangular and its case is made of plastic.
The Fitbit Edge comes in four stock colors (olive green, black, white and a coral peach color), plus a pricier orange Steph Curry edition endorsed by the NBA star, while the Inspire 3 offers three stock colors (pink, orange and black). And while the Edge retails for $180, the Inspire 3 is 44% cheaper at $99.95. But if the Curry colorway is calling to you, it'll cost you $40 more than the base Edge model at $220.
More connectivity to leave the phone at home
Perhaps one of the best upgrades with the Fitbit Edge compared to the Inspire 3 is Edge's own built-in GPS, which Google says results in a 40 percent accuracy increase tracking your moves. This integrated GPS also means the Edge doesn't require your smartphone to be nearby to track your movement and location, so you can go on runs without having to bring it along.
Another important upgrade is the Edge's built-in Bluetooth 5.4 connection, so you can connect your wireless headphones directly to the watch. Both wearables support Google's "Find My Device" feature, as well as app notifications from your smartphone when nearby.
The Edge also supports Quick Replies, music controls and weather forecasts directly from your wrist. It's also expected to support Google Maps soon. The Inspire 3 doesn't have these features, but does support calendar notifications directly on-screen.
More fitness features
Both wearables can track your activity continuously, but the Edge was designed to support more exercise types and will automatically detect 100 different movement activities. Google says the Edge can track over 50 exercise modes, while the Inspire 3 can track 20.
New features the Edge offers that the Inspire 3 doesn't include tracking your "cardio load," "target cardio load," floors climbed and heart rate while using workout machines.
Track more of your health data
When it comes to heart health, the Fitbit Edge is able to offer more data than the Inspire 3. The Edge comes with 24/7 heart rate tracking and an ECG app that includes irregular heartbeat tracking (AFib detection). Edge can also give you monthly insights into your blood pressure and insulin resistance. And if you monitor your blood sugar separately, the Edge can help you analyze that data.
The Inspire 3 has an optical heart rate monitor, a blood oxygen tracker and an accelerometer for velocity, while the Edge comes with all of these plus sensors for the ECG app, a skin temperature sensor plus a gyroscope and altimeter for more accurate GPS tracking.
Shorter battery life, same water resistance
It might not come as a surprise that the Edge, with its larger screen and more features, has a shorter battery life on a single charge than the Inspire 3. But this likely won't be a dealbreaker for most, as Google says the Edge can go for up to a week on a single charge, while the Inspire 3 can last for up to 10 days on one charge. So if you plug it in a few times a week, you shouldn't notice a difference in battery life.
The Fitbit Edge and Inspire 3 rate the same for water resistance, with a 5 ATM under ISO standard 22810:2010 rating. This rating means that rain, showering or shallow-water swimming (like doing laps in a pool), but it's not likely to any diving.
The Edge has also been rated for dust resistance with an IP68 rating, while the Inspire 3 has not. This means the Edge is sealed from dust intrusion and can handle brief immersion in water. But like most electronics, neither devices are fully waterproof.
A middle ground between fitness tracker and smartwatch
Overall, the Fitbit Edge is a notable upgrade over the Inspire 3, with more premium materials, more trackable fitness data and less dependency on a smartphone. The Edge stands out as a middle-ground device that's somewhere between a simple fitness wearable and a fully-connected smartwatch that can make calls on its own. So if the Google Pixel Watch 5's price tag and features feel like a bit too much for your needs, the Edge is one way to get the fitness tracking you need with fewer distractions.

title_en: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix’s OpenAI hack documentary isn’t accurate
title_fa: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix’s OpenAI hack documentary isn’t accurate
excerpt_en: Before you share the Netflix documentary "AI Gone Rogue," take note. Clem Delangue, Hugging Face's co-founder who is featured in the film, says it went "full doomer mode" and isn't accurate.
excerpt_fa: Before you share the Netflix documentary "AI Gone Rogue," take note. Clem Delangue, Hugging Face's co-founder who is featured in the film, says it went "full doomer mode" and isn't accurate.
content_en:
Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown, take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents.
“Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X. “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.”
To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well, including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened.
In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment and spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible.
But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack.
In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”
Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.”
But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.
The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack.
But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote.
It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on-screen.
Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!”
In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take.

But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack.
In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”
Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.”
But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.
The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack.
But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote.
It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on-screen.
Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!”
In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take.

title_en: Trump is giving Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million fraud bounty program
title_fa: Trump is giving Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million fraud bounty program
excerpt_en: Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday that the Trump administration was giving right-wing YouTuber Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million bounty program for members of the public to report fraud. In December 2025, Shirley published a viral video...
excerpt_fa: Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday that the Trump administration was giving right-wing YouTuber Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million bounty program for members of the public to report fraud. In December 2025, Shirley published a viral video...
content_en:
Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday that the Trump administration was giving right-wing YouTuber Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million bounty program for members of the public to report fraud.
Trump is giving Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million fraud bounty program
In December 2025, Shirley published a viral video alleging fraud at daycares in Minnesota that were operated by members of the local Somali community. Shirley lingered in parking lots and asked to enter childcare centers, taking refusals as evidence that the centers weren’t actually caring for children. The video quickly went viral, triggering a massive governmental response: Federal immigration agents descended on the Minneapolis area, and the Trump administration froze Minnesota’s federal funding for childcare. Shirley has since visited other states in the US under similar pretenses, showing up unannounced to grocery stores and hospice centers in search of evidence of fraud. Vance and others in the administration publicly praised Shirley, who has since become a mainstay in the MAGA-aligned content creator ecosystem. He’s helped popularize a genre of so-called independent journalism popular on the right in which content creators and influencers confront businesses or people they suspect of fraud or crime as the basis for their online content. Harassment — or even immigration crackdowns — often follow.
The administration told Fox News that it was also launching the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program (WHIP), a pool of $25 million open to anyone who believes they’ve witnessed fraud. A “particular emphasis” is placed on fraud in hospice, home healthcare, daycares, and special services, a government website says. A chatbot collecting responses instructs the reporting party: “Briefly describe what you saw, heard, or read. A few sentences are enough. Include names, dates, amounts, or records if you have them, and how you know. Note any details you’re unsure about.”
According to Fox News and the reporting portal, members of the public who flag fraud are eligible to get up to $30,000 if a tip submitted leads to a conviction or significant federal action. But speaking on Tuesday, Trump contradicted the $30,000 ceiling.
”If you turn somebody in and … you find $1 billion, we are giving a commission to that person of 1 percent,” Trump said today. (One percent of $1 billion would exceed the $30,000 cap.) “And if it’s $10 billion, $200 billion, $400 billion, we’re giving a 1 percent commission to that person,” Trump continued.
The White House didn’t immediately clarify how the $10,000 payment to Shirley was calculated or how the program is being funded in the first place.
Shirley’s methods have been criticized particularly in Minnesota, where sweeping fraud investigations were already taking place before he arrived to make content. He accused businesses of faking childcare services based on little more than being denied entry to facilities, and — to the frustration of many — acted as if his video was the first fraud investigation in the state. Subsequent state official visits to the centers Shirley featured found them operating “as expected.”

title_en: Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car
title_fa: Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car
excerpt_en: Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search. As an example, Google says...
excerpt_fa: Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search. As an example, Google says...
content_en:
Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search.
Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car
Gemini AI can now draw from Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, and other apps while you drive.
Gemini AI can now draw from Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, and other apps while you drive.
As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.”
Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps.
Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says.
Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

title_en: The next Xbox might cost $1,800, report says
title_fa: The next Xbox might cost $1,800, report says
excerpt_en: Microsoft is targeting a 2028 release for its next-gen Xbox, which could be incredibly expensive, according to details reported in a profile with Xbox's CEO.
excerpt_fa: Microsoft is targeting a 2028 release for its next-gen Xbox, which could be incredibly expensive, according to details reported in a profile with Xbox's CEO.
content_en:
The next Xbox might cost $1,800, report says
Project Helix could break the bank due to high part costs and shortages.
Fortune published a lengthy profile of new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma that included some snippets of information about the company's upcoming plans. The much-discussed Project Helix, Xbox's a next-gen gaming console that will also play PC games, got some mentions, including potential pricing and release timing. The next hardware release from Xbox is reportedly a handheld device that's slated to arrive for the 2027 holiday season, with the full console to come in the same time period during 2028.
In a different interview in August, Sharma hinted that Project Helix would be a "family" of gaming devices, so the news of multiple releases isn't a surprise. The more shocking development is around price. Fortune reported that the Project Helix console is currently projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 unless Microsoft opts to subsidize the hardware.
If that does turn out to be the going rate, and it definitely could be given the ongoing explosion in prices for RAM and other components driven by AI development, it might be a major roadblock for Sharma's goal of seeing Xbox reach more than 1 billion people daily.
A lot could still change in the next two years. It's possible this high figure is being teased so that when the actual price is lower, Microsoft and Xbox might appear more benevolent toward customers. Or the price really will be that eye-poppingly high, and Xbox will face a steep climb to grow from its current reported level of 100 million daily active users. It's hard to imagine people shelling out that much for hardware from the beleaguered brand when they could opt for the currently cheaper Steam Machine.
Another detail shared with Fortune includes a potential overhaul of Xbox's Game Pass to have a la carte pricing with add-ons for "console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer," according to unnamed insiders. The next rounds of layoffs in Xbox's ongoing downsizing effort are also expected to come this month, followed by additional cuts planned for November and January.

title_en: What to expect at Apple's 'Pro and Tell' event on October 28
title_fa: What to expect at Apple's 'Pro and Tell' event on October 28
excerpt_en: From the first touchscreen MacBook to an OLED iPad mini, here's everything Apple is expected to announce next week.
excerpt_fa: From the first touchscreen MacBook to an OLED iPad mini, here's everything Apple is expected to announce next week.
content_en:
What to expect at Apple's 'Pro and Tell' event on October 28
From the first touchscreen MacBook to an OLED iPad mini, here's everything Apple is expected to announce next week.
Following the launch of the HomeView and other smart home products last week, Apple has now confirmed its third product event of the season. Invitations bearing the tagline "Pro and Tell" went out this week, and the showcase will take place on October 28 in Los Angeles. However, it won't be a traditional event, but rather a briefing for the press and creators. As usual, Apple doesn't reveal in advance which products it will announce, but all signs point to two main categories: Mac and iPad. If the rumors are true, we'll see the first MacBook with an OLED display and touchscreen, and the M6 chip coming to more Macs. In addition, the iPad mini might also get a major update with an OLED display and a faster chip. Here's everything to expect from next week's event.
A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen
The star of the show is expected to be a new MacBook Pro, which will is supposed to be the first Mac with a touchscreen. Rumors suggest it will come in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes like the current models — but they may end up looking quite different. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman recently reported that this new MacBook could be thinner and lighter, while the OLED display should allow for thinner bezels and a hole-punch camera cutout with a Dynamic Island instead of a notch. Chances are this will be the biggest redesign of the MacBook Pro since the versions that were introduced in 2021.
However, don't expect to see the new M6 chip inside it. Gurman's sources claimed that Apple will stick with the current M5 Pro and M5 Max, rather than switching to the M6 family. If you were hoping for a faster MacBook Pro, you'll likely have to wait until 2027, when Apple is rumored to refresh its high-end laptop with the M7 Pro and M7 Max chips. This Mac won't come cheap either, according to a report by Macworld. It probably won't be a successor to existing models, but rather an even more expensive version that expands the lineup. The current models without touchscreens should remain available for those not wanting to pay the higher price.
M6 chips come to more Macs
Although the touchscreen MacBook won't get the M6 chip, other Macs will. The M6 was introduced in August with the latest Mac mini, and now other Macs are rumored to be getting it as well. The leading candidate is the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro — Apple did something similar last year with the M5 version. Don't expect a touchscreen, OLED display or any design changes in this version, though. The only upgrade should be the M6 chip, which offers improved performance and lower power consumption.
The iMac is also a strong candidate for an update next week, especially since the current model was introduced in 2024 and still runs on the M4 chip. Here, the M6 chip is expected to mark an even more significant jump, with much better CPU and GPU performance. The M6 also comes with a dual 16-core Neural Engine, which runs AI tasks much faster. We may also see new color options available, although the design will remain the same.
An iPad mini with OLED
Macs likely won't be the only products getting an update at next week's event. The iPad mini is also expected to get some spotlight with a new generation, and this will be a big one, too. Apple is reportedly adding an OLED display to the iPad mini for the first time. Current models still have LCD screens. If true, the mini will be the first iPad besides the iPad Pro to feature an OLED display.
Another upgrade should be the A20 Pro chip, which is already in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Currently, the iPad mini still runs on the A17 Pro chip from the iPhone 15 Pro — and is known for heating up a lot. Other rumors about the new iPad mini include thinner bezels around the screen, a relocated front-facing camera and some level of water resistance for the first time. Of course, none of these details have been confirmed yet, so we'll find out what Apple has to share for sure on October 28.

title_en: The latest PlayStation firmware may have already been cracked ahead of GTA 6
title_fa: The latest PlayStation firmware may have already been cracked ahead of GTA 6
excerpt_en: Hackers aren't giving up at cracking the Playstation 5's latest firmware as evidenced by a new video showing an apparent kernel exploit.
excerpt_fa: Hackers aren't giving up at cracking the Playstation 5's latest firmware as evidenced by a new video showing an apparent kernel exploit.
content_en:
The latest PlayStation firmware may have already been cracked ahead of GTA 6
A firmware exploit does not mean the game can be pirated, though.
Sony's latest PlayStation 5 firmware (14.10.00) appears to have been cracked, based on a video shared by a developer named "Gezine" on X. The video shows Gezine navigating through the PS5's hidden Debug Settings, menus that are typically only available if you have kernel-level access to the console's operating system.
A possible exploit for the PS5's latest firmware is notable both because Sony released the software update in October, and because the firmware is reportedly necessary to play the year's biggest release. According to datamining by X account PlayStation Game Size, Grand Theft Auto VI requires the latest firmware to run, theoretically blocking it from being played on jailbroken consoles running older firmware. It was possible to jailbreak the console and play illegally obtained copies of games using the "Relapse" jailbreak on earlier PS5 firmware, but the update to 14.10 closed that loophole — until now.
Hello 14.10 pic.twitter.com/D7prKmOkbD
— Gezine (@gezine_dev) October 19, 2026
Of course, just because a developer has found a kernel exploit for the console's firmware doesn't mean GTA VI itself is any closer to being ripped or ported to another platform. Gezine has not publicly shared their method for hacking the PS5's firmware. In fact, in a reply to their original post sharing the video of the console's debug menus, they said they were "gonna ask for disclosure later," suggesting they may report it to a bug bounty program first. Sony hasn't acknowledged this hack, but the company does run a bug bounty program that pays security researchers for identifying similar ones.
A kernel exploit is also only one of the ingredients necessary to "unlock" a digital game for use elsewhere. A new hypervisor exploit — a hack of the software security layer running under the kernel — would be necessary to crack games or run other illegal copies. At least so far, that exploit hasn't materialized. Without it, Grand Theft Auto VI will only be available through a traditional physical or digital purchase. And, unlike with past games, even physically purchasing the new GTA only gets you a download code and a game box. The game's console exclusivity, at least for now, is one reason players might be interested in playing a cracked version. The more obvious reason is to avoid paying $80.

title_en: Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, Musk says
title_fa: Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, Musk says
excerpt_en: Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter's third quarter earnings call Tuesday. Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees were formed at the request of shareholders and consist of...
excerpt_fa: Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter's third quarter earnings call Tuesday. Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees were formed at the request of shareholders and consist of...
content_en:
Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter’s third quarter earnings call Tuesday.
Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, Musk says
Musk called the merger “a good idea,” though he cautioned it wasn’t a guarantee.
Musk called the merger “a good idea,” though he cautioned it wasn’t a guarantee.
Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees were formed at the request of shareholders and consist of independent directors (though he did not name them). He also noted that he is not a member of either committee, nor involved in any of the discussions.
“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” Musk said. “So it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation.”
The groups have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction — and there’s no guarantee that they will. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” he continued. “And particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50 percent vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that’s quite a high hurdle to try to achieve.”
That said, Musk called the possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger a “good idea.” He continued:
I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity. And there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the TeraFab, obviously robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity. So I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies. They’ve got to come up with something and then that’s going to be put to the shareholders as a vote.
A Tesla-SpaceX merger would be a blockbuster corporate deal creating a mega-entity valued upwards of $3.6 trillion. To buy SpaceX, Tesla would have to create millions of new stock shares, which for current Tesla owners would mean owning a smaller slice of a much larger pie. SpaceX’s launch goals require tens of billions of dollars every year — extra spending that could drain Tesla’s ability to build new car factories and battery plants.
That said, most Wall Street analysts and legal experts believe SpaceX would acquire Tesla (or absorb it through a stock swap) rather than vice versa. Since its IPO, SpaceX has maintained a higher valuation than Tesla. A merger in that direction would allow SpaceX shareholders to hold the majority control of the combined mega-entity. Some Tesla shareholders may balk at this deal.
But it would also create one company for those who believe in Musk’s vision of the future — robot cars, humanoid robots, AI super-intelligence, and human habitats on Mars — in which to place their investments. And Tesla shareholder approved Musk’s enormous pay package last year — even after a Delaware judge tossed it over lack of independence.
Earlier this month, Barclays published a client note suggesting a potential Tesla-SpaceX combination could be announced ahead of Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting scheduled for December 3, 2026.

title_en: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
title_fa: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
excerpt_en: Anthropic is reportedly struggling to secure enough compute from cloud providers that increasingly view it as a competitor, even as its infrastructure spending balloons ahead of a planned November IPO.
excerpt_fa: Anthropic is reportedly struggling to secure enough compute from cloud providers that increasingly view it as a competitor, even as its infrastructure spending balloons ahead of a planned November IPO.
content_en:
Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal.
The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more than $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which include deals still in negotiation.
And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.
Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.
Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.
Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion, up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

title_en: ChatGPT now lets you lock sensitive chats behind a PIN
title_fa: ChatGPT now lets you lock sensitive chats behind a PIN
excerpt_en: OpenAI has introduced a new "locked chats" feature to protect users' more sensitive conversations with ChatGPT.
excerpt_fa: OpenAI has introduced a new "locked chats" feature to protect users' more sensitive conversations with ChatGPT.
content_en:
ChatGPT now lets you lock sensitive chats behind a PIN
Locked chats aren't a form of end-to-end encryption, however.
OpenAI is making it easier to protect your ChatGPT conversations from prying eyes with the introduction of a feature called locked chats. With it enabled, you can decide whether a past exchange appears in your regular chat history, pinned chats and conversation search. To access your locked chats, you'll need to input a 4-digit PIN. On an iPhone or Android phone, you can also use authentication systems like Face ID to access those conversations. Either way, you'll find your private conversations grouped under a new project titled "Locked chats."
OpenAI envisions locked chats mostly as a way to prevent people in public or someone you hand your phone to from seeing your conversations with ChatGPT. What they aren't is a form of end-to-end encryption or a way to skirt OpenAI's legal obligations if you get in trouble with your workplace or the law. The company says so explicitly in a newly published support page, where it also notes locked chats won't automatically change your model training settings, or how long OpenAI retains your private conversations. That said, if you need to reset your account PIN for any reason, doing so will delete all of your locked chats, alongside any files you've uploaded to their project space. "This cannot be undone, and OpenAI Support cannot recover the deleted content," the company warns.
OpenAI says it's rolling out locked chats to users gradually. If you don't see the option right away, it may take a few days before it arrives in your account. Availability will extend to free accounts, as well as to those with Go, Plus and Pro subscriptions. On Android and iOS, you can use voice mode in combination with locked chats, though you can't lock your Codex conversations behind the feature.

title_en: SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster for first time, Musk says
title_fa: SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster for first time, Musk says
excerpt_en: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company would attempt to catch Starship and its booster next month, with the goal of recovering the entire orbital launch system for the first time. If successful, Musk said, the attempt would mark the first time in history an orbital launch vehicle...
excerpt_fa: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company would attempt to catch Starship and its booster next month, with the goal of recovering the entire orbital launch system for the first time. If successful, Musk said, the attempt would mark the first time in history an orbital launch vehicle...
content_en:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company would attempt to catch Starship and its booster next month, with the goal of recovering the entire orbital launch system for the first time. If successful, Musk said, the attempt would mark the first time in history an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered.
SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster for first time, Musk says
If successful, it would be the first time in history an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered.
If successful, it would be the first time in history an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered.
“This is a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization consciousness,” he said during the company’s third quarter earnings report Tuesday.
But he also allowed for the possibility of a failure. “Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight,” Musk said. “And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year and then accelerating next year.”
“Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.”
— Elon MuskStarship is a two-stage system, composed of the Super Heavy booster (first stage) and the Starship spacecraft (second stage). It stands approximately 120 meters (around 400 feet) tall with a 9-meter diameter, and is powered by SpaceX’s Raptor engines burning liquid methane and liquid oxygen. Starship, which was first introduced in 2018, was designed to return to the launch site, where launch towers with mechanical “chopstick” arms catch the vehicle mid-air.
Last month’s Starship launch represented two firsts for its next gen rocket: send the spacecraft into Earth orbit, and insert a few dozen of SpaceX’s larger and more capable V3 satellites into the Starlink constellation for the first time. Still, the launch wasn’t without its snafus: one Raptor engine shut down prematurely during ascent, prompting mission control to adapt and complete the climb on remaining. Because of the issue, SpaceX cut the planned 10-hour, 6-orbit mission short after about 3 hours and 2 Earth orbits.
The Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico, while the Starship upper stage executed a de-orbit burn and ended with a fiery vertical splashdown in the Pacific Ocean north of Hawaii. Neither piece was recovered.

title_en: Judge tosses sexual abuse lawsuit from Sam Altman's sister
title_fa: Judge tosses sexual abuse lawsuit from Sam Altman's sister
excerpt_en: A lawsuit brought by the OpenAI CEO's sister was dismissed after Anne Altman refused a medical exam.
excerpt_fa: A lawsuit brought by the OpenAI CEO's sister was dismissed after Anne Altman refused a medical exam.
content_en:
Judge tosses sexual abuse lawsuit from Sam Altman's sister
The case was dismissed over a refused medical exam, not on the merits.
A federal judge dismissed Ann Altman's lawsuit against her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, on Tuesday. US District Judge Zachary Bluestone didn't rule on the merits of her claims. Instead, he wrote that Ann refused to appear for an independent medical examination, despite being warned that skipping it would lead to the case's dismissal.
Ann Altman filed the lawsuit in January 2025, accusing Sam of sexually abusing her when she was a child. She alleged that the abuse took place at the family's Missouri home between 1997 and 2006, beginning when she was three and he was 12. She said the last instance of alleged abuse took place when her brother was an adult.
The case had already been revised once. In March, Bluestone ruled that Ann's original sexual assault and battery claims had expired years earlier. But the judge allowed her to refile under a Missouri childhood sexual abuse law. She then filed the amended suit that was dismissed on Tuesday.
The OpenAI CEO, now 41, has denied the claims. Bluestone also reportedly approved Sam Altman's request on Tuesday to withdraw a defamation counterclaim he made against his sister.
In a joint statement made after Ann Altman's initial lawsuit was filed, Sam Altman, his mother and two younger brothers called the allegations "entirely untrue." They claimed that Ann Altman had "mental health challenges" and "refuses conventional treatment and lashes out at family members who are genuinely trying to help."
Ann Altman's former lawyer, Santos Perez, who withdrew from the case in October, wrote in a statement, "I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie."

title_en: Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
title_fa: Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
excerpt_en: Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. As part of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, Netflix lists improvements to monetization as one of its main focuses going forward, alongside efforts to boost entertainment value and...
excerpt_fa: Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. As part of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, Netflix lists improvements to monetization as one of its main focuses going forward, alongside efforts to boost entertainment value and...
content_en:
Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. As part of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, Netflix lists improvements to monetization as one of its main focuses going forward, alongside efforts to boost entertainment value and leverage new technology.
Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
Improving monetization is one of Netflix’s top priorities.
Improving monetization is one of Netflix’s top priorities.
The streaming giant doesn’t say exactly how it plans to improve its monetization, but the company notes that these goals will help Netflix “create member value that lets us occasionally raise prices, and increase advertiser demand.” Netflix also highlighted plans to push further into original titles, live events, and third-party programming as it faces an “intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention.”
An analysis from financial firm Jefferies estimated that Netflix’s monthly viewing time per member dropped to 49 hours in the first half of this year, down from 66 hours in the first half of 2023, according to a report from Reuters. At the same time, Netflix made up 7.8 percent of US viewing time in the US in July, a one-percentage-point dip from the same time last year, The New York Times reports.
During an earnings call, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos pointed to success abroad when answering a question about the company’s content strategy. “We see titles across Latin America, EMEA (Europe, the Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia-Pacific), driving engagement, subscriber growth, revenue, and profit,” Sarandos said. “Now, the US is also working. It’s just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like.”
Last week, Netflix laid off around 1,000 employees, while replacing key executives, including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film head Dan Lin. Former Disney executive Peter Rice is taking over as chief content officer on October 26th. The Wall Street Journal recently reported that Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos complained internally that US-based users have been spending less time on the service, and that it’s “short on new hit shows.”
In its letter to investors, Netflix mentions its upcoming lineup of NFL games, its Grand Theft Auto VI preview, and its partnership with French TV station TF1 as evidence of opening its platform to a wider breadth of content. The company reported earning $12.9 billion over the past few months, marking a 12 percent year-over-year increase. It also plans to bring its ad-supported tier — which raked in $1.5 billion last year — to 15 new countries in 2027.
In the coming months, Netflix may be facing tougher competition from HBO Max and Paramount Plus following the Skydance megamerger, as co-CEO David Ellison has said that he plans to combine the two apps into a single service. The streamer struck deals with several creators as it competes with YouTube, which has reportedly offered channels “millions of dollars” not to post their videos on Netflix.
Netflix has also weighed making even bigger changes to its app, including integrating other third-party streamers, such as Peacock and Fox One, as well as adding always-on channels, according to reports from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.
Update, October 20th: Added a quote from Sarandos.

title_en: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
title_fa: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
excerpt_en: SpaceX hit profitability in the third quarter, with net income of $4.4 billion. AI was the engine.
excerpt_fa: SpaceX hit profitability in the third quarter, with net income of $4.4 billion. AI was the engine.
content_en:
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in the third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.
CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing.
That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.
The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.
The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.
During a livestreamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.
“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”
In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12- to 18-month delays in obtaining the metals that blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.
Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.
SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.
Despite those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.
Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”
More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.
This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.
