title_en: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
title_fa: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
excerpt_en: CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition - when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they'd get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath "SPAC King" Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and...
excerpt_fa: CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition - when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they'd get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath "SPAC King" Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and...
content_en:
CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too.
CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else.
When you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave is going to borrow even more
To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more.
“The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying.
I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit.
CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.
The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds
So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue.
Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business.
Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one.
Anyway, some people are buying the dip.

title_en: I tried a $99 plug that promises to track your car and send help when needed — without selling your data

excerpt_fa: My 15-year-old daughter just got her learner's permit, so when I was pitched a new gadget tailored to teen drivers, I was intrigued. The Miles Plug is a small device that plugs into your car's OBD-II port and monitors location, driving habits, and vehicle health, along with...
content_en:
My 15-year-old daughter just got her learner’s permit, so when I was pitched a new gadget tailored to teen drivers, I was intrigued. The Miles Plug is a small device that plugs into your car’s OBD-II port and monitors location, driving habits, and vehicle health, along with emergency accident response and roadside assistance.
I tried a $99 plug that promises to track your car and send help when needed — without selling your data
The Miles Plug adds crash detection, roadside help, location tracking, and a warning-light decoder to your car for as low as $11 a month.
The idea is that knowing all these things should help me feel more comfortable when my daughter starts driving alone. I tested the (now discontinued) Ring Car Cam when my son was learning to drive, but he hated it and refused to turn it on; I wondered if the Miles could provide the same peace of mind without feeling as intrusive.
Billed as “a wearable for your car,” Miles is a tiny cellular and GPS-enabled device that connects to an app to deliver real-time location, alerts, and driving insights (speeding, hard braking, trip recaps). The app also features an AI chatbot called the Miles Mechanic that decodes warning lights, tells you how urgent a fix is, and estimates repair costs.
Miles was developed by cofounders Matt McGovren and Kit Klein, who have a solid smart home pedigree. They worked at Wink in the early days and bring combined experience from Amazon (Ring and Blink), Ubiquiti’s smart home line, and other companies. “We built Miles to support teens and parents together, and keep them on the same team,” said McGovren in a press release. “Parents and teens see the same trips and the same alerts with nothing hidden, building trust instead of suspicion.”
You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product.
— Matt McGovrenMiles is available today at mileslabs.com and costs $99, plus $180 for a year of membership ($279 total, or $15 a month). A three-year plan is $396 with the Plug included ($11 a month). All plans are paid upfront with no auto-renewal. Anyone in the family can download and use the app, with each driver getting their own profile and alerts. Miles says it’s compatible with most gas and hybrid cars from 2008 onward and some EVs (there’s a compatibility checker).
While the prices seem steep, McGovren’s pitch is that it covers several services you might already be paying for: “You could piece together a roadside service, a family tracking service … and then you’re looking at $30, $40 a month,” he said in an interview with The Verge. And, unlike your car’s own branded app, Miles isn’t selling your data. Automakers have been caught collecting and selling driving data, with GM being banned from selling data to brokers for five years.
McGovren says Miles will never sell vehicle, trip, or location data, and the app has no ads: “You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product.” He says, “All the vehicle and trip data is encrypted,” adding that “the most sensitive data is end-to-end encrypted.” Additionally, the location data is tied to the car, not the phone, so it stops tracking when you walk away. The app lets you download your data, stop location collection, and delete your account and all its data.
I set up Miles in my 2014 Toyota Highlander I nicknamed Tanya and have been using it for a couple of days. Setup was simple, and the app is clean, uncluttered, and easy to follow. It took me through a few setup screens, including asking to share my phone’s location to relay data from the Plug over Bluetooth when cell service is spotty. I plugged it into my OBD-II port, and it read my VIN and correctly identified my car.
It logs every trip with route, distance, time, and driver initials (I haven’t had my daughter download the app yet; I’m interested to see whose phones it connects to when we’re both in the car). Arrived- and left-home alerts came through promptly, and the events tab flagged hard acceleration and a cluster of three hard-braking alerts when I was running a little late to collect my daughter from work.
I like the home card, which shows a vehicle health summary: engine OK, fuel 63%, battery 13.5V, and the odometer reading. I played with the Miles Mechanic chatbot and asked how my car is and what upcoming maintenance is due; it answered in plain English, telling me the cabin air filter is due at about 140,000 miles, and the oil change and tire rotation at 142,500.
I haven’t been testing it long enough to comment on battery drain, an issue with earlier products in this space. “It goes to sleep when your car is not driving or not on,” says McGovren. “We use a little bit of data to wake up and sync, but [that] doesn’t have a material impact on the battery.” He advises removing it if you won’t be driving the car for a while.
Beyond car battery life, an obvious concern for prospective users is how long Miles the company will last. Startup Automatic had a similar idea back in 2016, launching the Automatic Pro for $130 that plugged into your OBD-II port, tracked mileage and location, and monitored for crashes over a 3G radio. The service shut down in 2020. Miles is basically Automatic but with a business model; Automatic didn’t initially charge a monthly fee, Miles does.
McGovren says he and his team have seen a lot of “scar tissue from the smart home,” with companies that “thought they could make money later.” Both founders were at Wink during its outage, bankruptcy, and eventual sale to will.i.am’s company. Charging for membership upfront is meant to avoid that type of outcome. He says the company is “well capitalized” and offers a 60-day money-back guarantee to users.
The car becomes part of this bigger ecosystem. We aren’t just trying to tie you into our app.
— Matt McGovrenAutomatic also had several smart-home tie-ins, but at launch Miles doesn’t connect to your smart home. McGovren says they have an MCP server in beta that could deliver “all of this information …...

title_en: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
title_fa: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
excerpt_en: Amazon wants to break Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch, the free toolkit used to build most AI apps, so that more developers run their apps on alternative chips like its own.
excerpt_fa: Amazon wants to break Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch, the free toolkit used to build most AI apps, so that more developers run their apps on alternative chips like its own.
content_en:
On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.
TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.
Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.
TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.
However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.
“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”
AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.
“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.
But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.
Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote:
Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.
While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.
Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”
content_fa:
On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.
TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.
Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.
TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.
However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.
“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”
AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.
“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.
But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.
Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote:
Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.
While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.
Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

title_en: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts
title_fa: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts
excerpt_en: OpenCode is an open source AI coding agent that's become a popular alternative to Claude Code and Cursor. But hackers got into part of its online platform and stole some users’ API keys, and the AI tools it turned to for help kept refusing to look at the malicious code.
excerpt_fa: OpenCode is an open source AI coding agent that's become a popular alternative to Claude Code and Cursor. But hackers got into part of its online platform and stole some users’ API keys, and the AI tools it turned to for help kept refusing to look at the malicious code.
content_en:
OpenCode, an open source AI coding agent that has been gaining ground among developers as an alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, said Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight, affecting 1.4% of users of its online platform, OpenCode Console, where some users store the API keys, or digital passwords, they use to access AI services.
As the OpenCode team struggled to keep pace with the attack, the scramble to respond highlighted a growing problem: Companies without vetted access to AI models with fewer safety restrictions have a hard time defending against large-scale, AI-driven cyberattacks.
“We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the company wrote on X. “We have notified them all this morning via email.” Users who did not receive an email were not impacted, the company said.
While the company didn’t specify how the distillation attack occurred, leaked API keys can help users in countries with restricted access to American models generate the high volume of outputs needed for that process. Some skeptics called the framing an overstretch, arguing that the incident was a straightforward breach whose use for distillation remains unproven.
Overnight, developers began posting spending alerts and unauthorized charges on Reddit and X: “I saw my Open AI, Anthropic, and Google AI spend alerts all fire off before going to bed wondering what was going on,” a developer wrote.
Other users reported charges in the hundreds of dollars on individual accounts; a few described totals above $1,000.
Anthropic and Google both blocked the API keys they believed were exposed, while OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund its API customers for credits used in the attack. OpenCode said refunds for unauthorized charges are underway.
The exposed keys were confined to Console, where some users had them in workspaces. The open source app and command-line tool were not affected, according to co-founder Dax Raad. “Note this is the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself, those keys never come to us,” he wrote on X.
Even as users and AI companies moved to disable the exposed keys, the OpenCode team was still under pressure. Raad said attackers had been trying to break into its systems nonstop for 48 hours, requiring the team to keep AI defensive agents running around the clock. AI models that the OpenCode team turned to for analysis helped for a while, but started refusing to work when the malicious code they were asked to examine activated safety filters.
“[T]hat was a bit frustrating,” he wrote on X.
OpenCode later received access to OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users AI models that are less likely to refuse requests for defensive security work. Raad said the access improved the team’s ability to investigate the attack.
OpenCode isn’t the first company to hit this wall. In July, AI platform Hugging Face said commercial AI models blocked its attempts to analyze activity logs from an intrusion by autonomous AI agents, which OpenAI later revealed were its own models running with safeguards lowered during a test. In a section of its blog post titled “The asymmetry problem,” Hugging Face wrote that guardrails “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.”
Security researchers have raised similar complaints, saying the restrictions are inconsistent and have pushed some toward foreign open-weight models, which anyone can download and run.
The weekend episode drew a response from David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
“OpenCode (and earlier Hugging Face) hit the same wall mid-attack: frontier models refused to analyze the very exploits needed for defense because the payloads tripped safety filters. The guardrails backfired,” he wrote on X.
The breach occurred the same night OpenCode made GLM-5.3-Flash free for users. The broader GLM-5.3 family has drawn attention from researchers who study open-weight models and note that its cybersecurity capabilities approached levels previously associated with restricted-access models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Preview.
OpenCode has not detailed how attackers gained access to the older system, how keys were stored, or the full extent of any misuse. It has told affected users to revoke and replace their keys directly with each provider. The company said the incident remains ongoing.
The breach lands amid a run of AI-enabled cyber incidents. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said a China-based hacker likely used an AI penetration-testing agent, which probes computer systems for weaknesses, and Claude in attacks on South Korean banks. Last week, India’s cybersecurity agency warned that AI agents, including some being tested by AI companies, had reached Indian organizations’ systems without authorization.

title_en: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life
title_fa: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life
excerpt_en: AI companion app Tolan has raised another $30 million after attracting more than 250,000 active users.
excerpt_fa: AI companion app Tolan has raised another $30 million after attracting more than 250,000 active users.
content_en:
Tolan, the AI companion designed to help people manage their daily lives, navigate relationships and emotions, and accomplish their goals, has just expanded its runway with another $30 million in capital.
The startup’s investors in the latest round include Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling the total amount it has raised to date and pushing its valuation beyond the previous $120 million, according to a new report by Upstarts Media. (The startup didn’t disclose its new valuation, but PitchBook estimates it at more than $268 million, with “medium confidence.”)
Users engage with Tolan’s app through a cartoonish character that’s meant to offer support and help them get through their to-dos.
Tolan generates revenue from its tiered memberships, which are required for full access to all features. The company told Upstarts Media its annual recurring revenue is now in the “double-digit millions.”
The startup is one of the few AI companions that have found some traction, as it claims to have more than 250,000 active users who have had more than 70 million conversations over the past year. Around 70% of its users are women, and 40% are parents, Tolan’s team told the news outlet. (Anecdotally, the app is said to appeal in particular to neurodivergent people, who may benefit from additional support, whether that’s emotional support or help with organizing tasks.)
Compared with other companions, Tolan seems to have found a balance between being helpful without being perceived as too weird. Compare that with the public shaming that Friend’s pendant-based AI companion faced; users dubbed Friend “very cringe,” The New York Times called it “hated,” and Wired said it “has no soul.”
Meanwhile, another former top contender in the space, Character.AI, recently filed for bankruptcy after its founder’s return to Google. (Its remaining staff is transitioning to Disney, which bought some of its assets.)
However, Tolan could end up facing increased competition from the more recent crop of AI agents, which help users plan, organize, and accomplish their tasks and goals, not just talk their way through them. For instance, Meta gave its AI agent Muse a cute avatar for its users to talk to, which it also plans to release as a hardware product in the future.
The startup also has to navigate the risks of offering AI-powered emotional support, given that multiple lawsuits have been filed against general-purpose AI app makers alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to users’ suicides.

excerpt_fa: For a very limited time, Sony’s latest high-end noise-canceling earbuds are actually cheaper than their last-gen counterpart, the WF-1000XM5. B&H Photo is selling Sony’s latest WF-1000XM6 in black for an all-time low of $238 ($92 off) at checkout. Other retailers aren’t...
content_en:
For a very limited time, Sony’s latest high-end noise-canceling earbuds are actually cheaper than their last-gen counterpart, the WF-1000XM5. B&H Photo is selling Sony’s latest WF-1000XM6 in black for an all-time low of $238 ($92 off) at checkout. Other retailers aren’t currently offering a discount on the XM6.
Sony’s best noise-canceling earbuds are nearly $100 off today only
The flagship earbuds now cost about as much as their predecessor.
The flagship earbuds now cost about as much as their predecessor.
The XM6 are a solid upgrade over their predecessor and easily amongst the best noise-canceling wireless earbuds on the market. In his review, John Higgins noted that they do a better job of tuning out other people’s conversations than any other earbuds he’s tested. Sony has also improved the bone-conduction sensor and added AI-powered microphones that help keep your voice clear during calls, even in noisy environments.
The XM6 earbuds also deliver clean, balanced sound with impressive bass, raising the bar of what we expect with Sony’s WF-1000XM series. If you prefer to customize your listening experience, Sony’s Sound Connect app offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to adjust how much surrounding noise you hear without removing the earbuds. You can also personalize the touch controls.
The XM6 earbuds support Sony’s LDAC codec, which delivers higher-quality audio from compatible Android devices, too. New in the latest set is a listening mode that makes music sound more like background audio playing in a cafe, allowing you to listen to your favorite music without getting too distracted from whatever you’re doing.

title_en: Replika’s founder built the AI assistant she pitched at Disrupt 12 years ago
title_fa: Replika’s founder built the AI assistant she pitched at Disrupt 12 years ago
excerpt_en: Eugenia Kuyda's newest startup Wabi is positioned to take advantage of an idea she had more than a decade ago. Wabi offers a personal AI assistant with a twist, free and downloadable to anyone today.
excerpt_fa: Eugenia Kuyda's newest startup Wabi is positioned to take advantage of an idea she had more than a decade ago. Wabi offers a personal AI assistant with a twist, free and downloadable to anyone today.
content_en:
Twelve years ago today, Eugenia Kuyda stood up onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt and presented a conversational chatbot called IO that acted as a lifestyle concierge to help people book restaurants and vacations along with other tasks.
IO, the first product from her startup Luka, came before the deep learning breakthroughs that would eventually lead to today’s large language models. “It still worked,” Kuyda told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “It was pretty magical … but, of course, it’s nowhere near what we have today.”
Luka ended up becoming Replika, the popular AI chatbot companion company. Last year, Kuyda left as CEO of Replika and founded Wabi.
The technology has finally caught up with her original vision for Luka, just in time for Wabi to take on a wave of new personal AI assistants such as Muse and Instinct, which promise to do everything from manage your inbox to find you the best flight deals.
On Monday, Kuyda officially launched Wabi for all users, a multiplayer personal AI assistant that functions as a messenger app, allowing users to maintain multiple agentic threads dedicated to different tasks and long-term goals. Within each thread, users can build and use custom apps, like a weight-loss tracker inside a health thread or an app showing nearby children’s events inside a family thread.
The launch is something of a pivot for Wabi, though Kuyda describes it as more of an evolution. When TechCrunch covered Wabi’s initial launch last year, along with its $20 million pre-seed round, it was described as more of a social platform where you could create mini apps with prompts that you could share with friends or across the app.
Over the past year, Kuyda said the team realized that while people love personal software rather than “one size fits all solutions in the App Store,” they “maybe don’t want to spend a lot of time, or any time, building it.”
With Wabi 2.0, the agent decides what apps to build. The moment you connect it to your email, it automatically spins up a number of threads and apps to start with, and users can add to that by requesting custom apps or starting new threads.
“It’s doing what Instinct and Muse do, but it also has all these apps, which helps users do more stuff,” Kuyda said.
App-building isn’t Wabi’s only differentiator. Kuyda is also betting on its multithreaded, multiplayer design.
“It’s not just everything in one single thread like with Instinct and Muse, where you get buried in the information that it sends you every day,” Kuyda said. “Single thread experiences, if you think about it, get worse over time because it’s just so much context in one endless conversation.”
The longer an AI chatbot conversation goes on, the more likely it is to hallucinate, lose track of context, or respond in ways that would otherwise be blocked by safety guardrails, according to interviews with AI researchers.
Threads can also be shared, functioning as group chats.
“Today, all the agentic apps are just [conversations] between you and the agent, and I feel like it should be a lot more about bringing people together in a group chat together,” Kuyda said. “Not you doing it separately with your AI, and I’m doing it separately with my AI … I don’t think anyone has yet cracked multiplayer.”
Kuyda walked TechCrunch through some of her own shared threads. In one with her boyfriend, a row of apps along the top helps the two of them connect and find things to do together, including a live music tracker, an app that asks a question every day about their relationship, a running list of restaurant suggestions, important events from their shared calendar, and a list of books they’re reading together with suggestions for what to read next.
In her more family-focused thread, there is an app tracking her daughter’s schedule, another for finding kid-friendly events nearby, and another that quizzes her daughter on Japanese.
Within any shared chat, users can share as much or as little as they want, from email and calendar information to bank account details.
“So my partner can ask Wabi in the chat, ‘Is Eugenia free next Thursday?’ or ‘Did she buy those tickets?’” Kuyda said. She noted that access is scoped to individual chats, and everyone in a chat can see when someone’s personal information is requested.
On privacy more broadly, Wabi is SOC 2 compliant, meaning its data security controls have been independently audited. Wabi runs entirely in the cloud, and most user data is stored in the U.S., Kuyda said.
“My previous company Replika worked on AI that will make people feel … less lonely,” Kuyda said. “To a degree, that is [in Wabi] as well. AI can bring people together, even when it comes to just helping you spend time better together in real life, whether it’s going out and seeing a concert together or finding the next book that you will read together.”
Wabi is free for now, and the company hasn’t settled on a business model yet. Kuyda said Wabi is in talks to raise more funds.

excerpt_en: After drawing acquisition interest earlier this year, the Nvidia challenger raised $1.5 billion to remain independent.
excerpt_fa: After drawing acquisition interest earlier this year, the Nvidia challenger raised $1.5 billion to remain independent.
content_en:
Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on inference, has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion valuation. The round comes five months after the 10-year-old Nvidia challenger reportedly received acquisition interest from Intel and Qualcomm at valuations of as much as $5 billion.
The fresh round, which more than doubled Tenstorrent’s valuation from the $2.6 billion it fetched in late 2024, was led by Trace Capital, a new firm launched by Quiet Capital co-founder Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X. Other backers included Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price.
Jim Keller, a prominent microprocessor engineer and Tenstorrent CEO, told Bloomberg that the company decided to remain independent and raise more capital after it showed that its Galaxy servers could run DeepSeek models. The new capital will go toward scaling chips tailored for serving open-weight AI models and video generation.
Tenstorrent is part of a wave of AI hardware startups trying to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance. Among them is Etched, an AI chip maker that was fielding investment offers at valuations of $40 billion or more, TechCrunch reported earlier this month.

title_en: Here's how we would build out the perfect modular electric Slate truck
title_fa: Here's how we would build out the perfect modular electric Slate truck
excerpt_en: A Bronco for the modern age.
excerpt_fa: A Bronco for the modern age.
content_en:
Here's how we would build out the perfect modular electric Slate truck
Who wants a battery-powered 1970s throwback?
The Slate Truck is about as unique a vehicle as there is. The modular electric truck ships from the factory as a bare-bones two-seat pickup in a single (slate gray) color. But the fun begins when you trick it out with a catalog of over 200 add-ons. After hours of tinkering with the configurator, here's our ideal throwback build.
When customizing your Slate Truck, it helps to have a clear theme in mind. And what better theme than "1970s Ford Bronco"? Granted, no Bronco ever looked exactly like this. But if you concocted a blend of those old trucks and a modern EV, it might not be far off.
The catch? Once you add enough accessories to transform the Slate into something that fits your vision, the price may no longer be a selling point. While you can get the bare-bones version for $24,950, our build approaches $40,000 — and it will get even expensive after accounting for Slate's as-yet-unpriced accessories. The potential for upsell overspending is real, and you should know that going in.
The basics
Although it leaves the factory quite threadbare, the Slate Truck doesn't have to stay that way. You can turn it into a five-seat SUV (fastback or squareback) or a Jeep-like option that would pair well with an open-air back seat. We went with the squareback SUV, which brings the starting price up to $29,950 before accessories.
This includes a roll cage, extra airbags, a bench seat for three and the squared-off shell. That serves as a worthy foundation for our '70s-inspired build, since sleeker-looking fastback SUVs weren't around then. Plus, it's more practical for cargo and, even better, saves us $2,000.
Throwback style
While each Slate Truck starts as a muted gray, you can wrap it in a variety of colors. For our base, we went with the Michigan Copper full wrap ($670). This foundation evoked late '70s stylings more than other options.
After that, we added the Throwback body decal ($320) and Creamsicle shoulder decals ($190). This is what sells the nostalgic look, with the Atari-esque stripe running down the side. Slate also offers mirror and rocker accents, but the colors didn't fully match and risked overcrowding the side.
The front lamps, taillights and grille each get "Dots" plates. For under $160 total, they help the truck's face look a bit more era-appropriate.
Bronco on the outside
We also added an upgraded front bumper ($500) and rear bumper ($600), fog lights ($300), fender flares ($150), a spare tire carrier ($550) and running boards ($350). The bumpers and fog lights accentuate the squared-off look of old 4x4s, and the flares give it a wider, more aggressive appearance. Meanwhile, the running boards are a practical touch, making our lifted build easier to climb into.
That's thanks to the as-yet-unpriced lift kit, which reportedly adds about two inches of height. We paired that with all-terrain tires on 17-inch wheels ($1,100). Slate also sells 20-inch wheels, but the 17s' larger sidewalls, softer ride and more theme-appropriate look nudged things in their favor.
Although our build resembles something you could take off-road, a reality check is in order. This rear-wheel-drive truck is better suited to dirt roads and snowy driveways than steep trails or deep mud.
The roof rack completes the look
A boxy, '70s-style vehicle without a roof rack looks incomplete. So we added the squareback roof rack ($650) on Slate's T-rail ($125). The automaker also sells carriers for bikes, kayaks, skis and paddleboards that attach to it. There's even a roof basket for frequent campers.
Just keep in mind that Slate estimates just 205 miles of range for the base pickup, and our heavier SUV will likely be even worse. That doesn't lend itself to long road trips into the wilderness. We can only take our '70s Bronco cosplay so far.
Old and new on the inside
Lest you forget that you're riding in something nostalgic, the inside has similar references. The Throwback interior decal ($50)m Magma accents on the lower dash and climate knobs (both still unpriced) call back to the exterior side stripe, but without making the cabin too loud.
Everything else sticks with the stock dark interior. That includes added Slate Black armrests ($50 for the doors, with the console armrest's price still unannounced). On a more practical note, we threw in a center console ($250), door cubby organizers ($50) and all-weather floor liners for the front and back of the cabin ($135 total).
One thing we couldn't add: power windows. Although it's more Slate's choice than a nostalgic one, why not call it another ode to the past? Slate previously listed power windows but pulled them later, with a spokesperson saying they could eventually return.
A touch of tech
The Slate ships by default with no screen or stereo. The idea is to use your phone for both jobs, although add-ons can fill in some gaps.
That lack of built-in audio is one of the hardest limits for a music or podcast lover to get past. Fortunately, Slate gives you several accessory options, including a mount for Bluetooth speakers. We went with the center speaker ($250) plus a pair of front left and right speakers ($150). $400 seems like a reasonable enough price to pay for a modern sound system.
Then we added Slate's Bluetooth steering wheel controls (price TBD) to skip songs and answer calls without taking hands off the wheel. You can only pretend you're in the 1970s to a point.
Also in our build: the tablet mount (unpriced) alongside the standard phone mount. A larger screen for navigation was too hard to pass up. Although it isn't confirmed whether the mount can support it, we'd also look into one of those portable CarPlay / Android Auto displays to run car-specific apps.
We also added the Five Switch upgrade ($40) for a row of physical light switches. This accessory is required for the fog lights, which no wannabe Bronco should go without. We added the home charger...

title_en: We might finally know what's written on that mysterious plaque in Super Mario 64
title_fa: We might finally know what's written on that mysterious plaque in Super Mario 64
excerpt_en: The plaque's message has haunted the internet for 30 years.
excerpt_fa: The plaque's message has haunted the internet for 30 years.
content_en:
We might finally know what's written on that mysterious plaque in Super Mario 64
The plaque's message has haunted the internet for 30 years.
Super Mario 64 fans have been obsessing over a blurry plaque in the castle courtyard for over 30 years. We might finally know what's written on it, according to a report by Video Games Chronicle. This is thanks to a programmer who used open-source computational analysis software to get to the bottom of things.
This isn't graphical upscaling software. The image is simply too blurry for that. Even modern reissues still have that same blurry plaque, so that hasn't been a help to anyone.
Instead, programmer Mochi64 used the analysis engine to pore through millions of combinations of words and fonts, looking for something that matched the pixels in the plaque. The end result? Mochi64 believes the top of the plaque reads "Eternal Star" and the bottom reads "We hope so."
This isn't an absolute answer. Those are simply the two sentences that provided the closest possible match via the analysis software. There's still a chance it could be something else, but the software did make millions of comparisons.
There were several high-profile rumors throughout the 1990s and beyond that the plaque read "L is Real 2401." This was seen as a tease that Luigi was hiding somewhere in the game. IGN actually offered a $100 bounty to anyone who could figure out how to unlock Luigi and Nintendo Power even mentioned the "L is Real 2401" theory in an April Fool's Day issue.
Here's your only official footage of multiplayer Super Mario 64 from a Spaceworld 95 video kiosk as the camera clearly focuses on both charactershttps://t.co/cLCdSIl5B9 pic.twitter.com/RdtTGb8LpJ
— Yakumono (@LuigiBlood) December 15, 2023
This rumor was given new life when the game's director, Shigeru Miyamoto, noted that the team had been experimenting with a two-player mode. He also said that they gave up on the idea to conserve memory, but that didn't stop the rumor mill. An early build showing Mario and Luigi running around a bare room didn't help things.
So there you have it. The phrase "Eternal Star" makes sense, as the plaque sits below a giant star statue. Perhaps the second sentence of "We hope so" indicates that the developers wanted players to collect every star. In any event, it's highly unlikely we'll ever get official confirmation from Nintendo.

title_en: AI assistant startup Town nabs unicorn valuation 4 months after launch
title_fa: AI assistant startup Town nabs unicorn valuation 4 months after launch
excerpt_en: AI assistant startup Town nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures.
excerpt_fa: AI assistant startup Town nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures.
content_en:
Town, a two-year-old, San Francisco-based startup developing AI assistants, nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B funding round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures. The company launched publicly just four months ago and said it reached millions of dollars in annual recurring revenue in a matter of weeks. It has raised at least $160 million to date, having previously announced a $55 million Series A round in June.
Town — founded by former Plaid CTO Jean-Denis Greze — is one of many AI assistants flooding the market right now. Town targets businesses, giving each employee an AI assistant called a Townie that helps with tasks by connecting to tools such as emails and calendars, as well as other core work systems. Employees’ Townies can talk to each other and share approved information; they can also now work with customers and others outside the company.
Alongside the funding, Town announced a shared workflow that automatically updates employees’ Townies with new business information rather than requiring each worker to update their own Townie. Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures, and First Round Capital also participated in the round.
We’ve reached out to the company for comment.

title_en: Is paid antivirus actually a waste of money for your PC in 2026?
title_fa: Is paid antivirus actually a waste of money for your PC in 2026?
excerpt_en: Subscribing to an antivirus suite kept you safe a long time ago, but they're much less useful for most people today.
excerpt_fa: Subscribing to an antivirus suite kept you safe a long time ago, but they're much less useful for most people today.
content_en:
Is paid antivirus actually a waste of money for your PC in 2026?
Windows has great protection built-in, so third-party suites come down to the extras.
Windows was not the safest operating system in the early days. Back then, malware and viruses were a risk that you were required to avoid and resolve on your own. As attacks grew, a whole antivirus industry spun up to provide protection for millions of PC users. Suites like McAfee, AVG and Norton were common options people installed to keep their computers safe.
Times have moved on, though. We've had built-in antivirus protection on PCs since Windows 8 launched in 2012. But third-party antivirus software still exists, along with apps offering more complex anti-malware protection. While there can be uses for these other tools, protection is now baked into your PC from the first day you boot, so you don't need to pay for it.
Windows' built-in antivirus protection is now pretty good
It took a few years for Microsoft Defender Antivirus to become something you can rely on. If you roll back 11 years and look at AV-Test's May–June 2015 testing, Defender scored just 0.5 out of six for the quality of its protection. Compare that to results from July-August 2026, where Defender earned the full six point. It detected 100 percent of threats in both the real-world attack and widespread malware tests, compared with industry averages of 99.9 percent and 100 percent each. Independent testing doesn't guarantee you'll have the same experience, but these real-world scenarios give you an idea of how Defender will react to threats your PC might face.
In Windows 11, Microsoft Defender Antivirus is a core part of the Windows Security suite. It'll scan your PC automatically, checking files and apps as you access them. Regular security updates mean you won't have to remember to download new malware definitions, either.
Defender will work in the background, but if you need to scan a file on-demand right-click it, choose Show more options if necessary, then hit Scan with Microsoft Defender. You're able to check for more threats in the Windows Security app by Virus & threat protection > Quick scan, with other ways to check for malware under the Scan options section.
Paid security suites can prove useful in some cases
In 2026, true viruses aren't the only (or even most common) threat you'll face on your PC. There are fake login pages designed to steal your passwords, scam emails that tell you to pay an invoice and fake security pop-ups claiming you need to call a phone number because your PC is at risk. All this, and plenty more, tries to trick you into making a mistake.
This is where the modern antivirus industry now lies: extras. Most third-party antivirus software has a free tier for core protection, but that's just one component in wider security subscriptions that offer various layers of protection. Anti-scam tools, VPNs, password managers and more are all bundled in to give you a reason to subscribe. Malwarebytes, for instance, advertises additional ransomware and anti-exploit protection in its paid plan. Norton's 360 Deluxe plan, meanwhile, includes a VPN, parental controls and 50GB of cloud backup storage. These plans often cover the whole family, with apps for smartphones and other devices.
These aren't completely useless; a full security suite could be useful if you're helping someone who struggles to spot scams and other online dangers. Those additional warnings and blocks can help, and the additional security layers of a VPN (if it's good enough) can also help protect your data online, especially if blocks ads and trackers.
The question is whether you'll actually use what's included, and a lot of people will likely not. Malwarebytes' free app is good as a second-opinion scanner; combined with 24/7 Microsoft Defender protection, you don't need to pay an extra cent to have a solid level of coverage on your PC. If you want to use tools like a VPN or password manager, you'll find dedicated, more reliable options. Our Norton VPN review found it lacking compared to others, for instance.
Your browser likely has additional protection built-in for free. Microsoft Edge, for example, has SmartScreen protection, which automatically checks websites you visit for any reports of phishing or malware. It'll also warn you about potentially dangerous downloads. It's an important reminder that security software is only one of the pillars of online safety.
Don't keep paying for antivirus software out of habit
If you've been using PCs for decades, subscribing to an antivirus program might feel like something you're supposed to do. That was understandable when Windows had little built-in protection, but it's time to reconsider. If you pay for a full security suite, how many of those extras have you actually used? Browser add-ons and maintenance utilities add bloat to your system.
The free versions of third-party AV tools can also be a pain. Constant pop-ups about minor issues or prompts to upgrade make the software feel like an ongoing sales pitch. These companies need paid subscribers, while Microsoft has a clear interest in keeping Windows safe by default. That's why Microsoft Defender Antivirus doesn't nag you unless there's a problem. You can't run both, either. Installing a third-party antivirus with real-time protection usually results in Defender switching itself off to keep conflicts at a minimum.
You'll also need to think about performance. Third-party antivirus software isn't going to automatically slow down your PC, but Tom's Guide found that running a full scan with Malwarebytes Premium dropped Cyberpunk 2077's performance down from 87 to 75 fps on its test PC. Bitdefender had a smaller impact, dropping from 100 to 97 fps during a full scan.

You can't run both, either. Installing a third-party antivirus with real-time protection usually results in Defender switching itself off to keep conflicts at a minimum.

Bitdefender had a smaller impact, dropping from 100 to 97 fps during a full scan.
Third-party protection still has merit and there are reasons why it might work for you. But for most people, it's almost certainly a waste of money. Windows doesn't need third-party protection against viruses or standard...

title_en: Rivian’s CEO says autonomy will enable ‘dramatically different’ vehicle designs
title_fa: Rivian’s CEO says autonomy will enable ‘dramatically different’ vehicle designs
excerpt_en: Founder and CEO RJ Scaringe said he thinks autonomy will allow his company to build radically different kinds of vehicles than the outdoorsy SUVs and trucks it currently makes.
excerpt_fa: Founder and CEO RJ Scaringe said he thinks autonomy will allow his company to build radically different kinds of vehicles than the outdoorsy SUVs and trucks it currently makes.
content_en:
Rivian is going full steam ahead on developing autonomous vehicle software for its EVs, to the point that it is willing to delay profitability. Founder and CEO RJ Scaringe said last week at TechCrunch Disrupt that he thinks autonomy will allow his company to build radically different kinds of vehicles than the outdoorsy SUVs and trucks it currently makes.
“Where it gets really interesting is when you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities. It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.”
This is not a new idea, to be sure. A decade ago, autonomous vehicle companies, legacy automakers, and many others promised that autonomy, combined with the proliferation of battery-electric drivetrains (which are simpler and take up less space than their gas-powered predecessors), would produce a Cambrian explosion of new mobility form factors.
This led to all kinds of crazy concepts getting bandied about at the time. Mercedes-Benz touted a bubbly pod-like design, as well as a long sedan packed with tech. Toyota and others dreamed up “rooms on wheels.” Hyundai once even showed off its idea for a car with legs.
This promised design revolution never escaped the concept and prototyping phase. Autonomy took longer than those companies anticipated to develop, and automakers (new and old) struggled with the harsh realities of manufacturing and selling an entirely new category of vehicle.
The difference now is that Scaringe’s comments come at a time when there are real robotaxis roaming the streets of multiple cities around the world. The software that powers them has seemingly developed to a level that is capable enough to operate them safely on public roads at scale, even if there are still some issues to work out when it comes to integrating them into the urban fabric of cars, bikes, pedestrians, and emergency vehicles. The components that make up electric vehicle motors and batteries have gotten cheaper, and companies like Tesla and Rivian (and many more in China) have gotten better at building them at scale.
Rivian has a lot of work ahead before it gets to driverless vehicles. The company is at the beginning of its effort to scale production of the R2 SUV, which it needs to get right in order to reverse years of losses that it incurred to become a major EV player.
On the autonomy side, Rivian is just a few years removed from completely reworking its approach to self-driving software, and it still has a ways to go.
The company has shipped a driver-assistance system that allows drivers to take their hands off the wheel, while still watching the road. It has promised that, by the end of this year, that software will be capable of driving from start to finish — which the company calls “point-to-point navigation” — without intervention, though still under driver supervision. And it is working toward full autonomy, which it plans to deploy in robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV that will be available on Uber’s ride-hail app.
But if Rivian achieves full autonomy, most of that driving will be done in personally owned vehicles, Scaringe said in the interview, echoing previous comments he’s made.
“You know, 95% of the miles driven in the United States — so this is trillions of miles — 95% of these miles are in things that we personally own, so like you own it, or your household owns it. And so our view is it’s unlikely, even with Level 4 capabilities, that we’re going to see a dramatic societal shift away from that,” he said, referencing the Society of Automotive Engineers’ classification for autonomous vehicles that operate in a specific area.
That figure “may go from 95% to 90%, it may go from 95% to 80%, but still the vast majority of the miles driven for a lot of societal and psychological reasons are likely to stay the same,” he said.
It’s this belief that has Scaringe dreaming about the design of a fully autonomous, personally owned Rivian, he said.
As for what that looks like, though, Scaringe was mum.
“So we did R1, then we did R2, then we did R3. The thing after R3 is going to be called R4 — we just haven’t shown what it looks like,” he said. “It’s going to be cool. It’s going to be great.”

title_en: Homeland Security bans DeepSeek use in federal civilian agencies
title_fa: Homeland Security bans DeepSeek use in federal civilian agencies
excerpt_en: The decision comes a couple of days after the release of Deepseek's latest AI model.
excerpt_fa: The decision comes a couple of days after the release of Deepseek's latest AI model.
content_en:
Homeland Security bans DeepSeek use in federal civilian agencies
The decision comes a couple of days after the release of the company’s latest AI model.
The Department of Homeland Security has issued a sweeping restriction to remove DeepSeek use across all federal civilian agencies and their IT systems. In a notice published with the Federal Register, DHS characterized the risks of DeepSeek use as potentially resulting in the "transfer of sensitive data" of US government employees and vendors to the Chinese government.
Following the order, civilian agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency or Federal Communications Commission would have to exclude any DeepSeek products from being used, while also removing any existing related products. DHS said in the notice that DeepSeek's models could "contain malware or other security vulnerabilities." The notice also disallows DeepSeek from participating in any federal government contracts.
DHS' order comes on the heels of DeepSeek releasing its latest model, V4.1-Flash-1017, which the company called "smarter, faster, more efficient." However, it's not the first time that the Chinese AI company has run into friction with the US government, especially at a time when its cheaper AI models start to rival the likes of ChatGPT or Gemini. Last year, two US Congressmembers proposed a bill that would ban DeepSeek's AI chatbot from government devices.

title_en: Amazon to fund 12 small nuclear reactors at former Indiana coal plant
title_fa: Amazon to fund 12 small nuclear reactors at former Indiana coal plant
excerpt_en: Amazon and X-energy have inked another deal to deploy nuclear power to the grid. This one will generate nearly 1 gigawatt of electricity.
excerpt_fa: Amazon and X-energy have inked another deal to deploy nuclear power to the grid. This one will generate nearly 1 gigawatt of electricity.
content_en:
Amazon is funding development of a proposed 960-megawatt nuclear plant in Indiana and would be the first customer to buy its power, the companies announced Monday. Utility company American Electric Power (AEP) would operate the plant. X-energy, which designs small modular nuclear reactors and went public in April, would supply the reactors.
The new power plant would consist of 12 Xe-100 small modular reactors and be located on the site of a demolished coal power plant just south of Terre Haute. The deal is the second commercial agreement between Amazon and X-energy, and it’s three times larger than the first, which was announced two years ago.
Amazon has invested heavily in X-energy, leading a $700 million Series C-1 round in October 2024. The two companies have said they ultimately plan to build 5 gigawatts of new nuclear generating capacity in the U.S. by 2039.
Unlike many newly announced power plants, these reactors would be connected to the public electric grid, though Amazon says the power would also serve its data centers.
The companies’ aggressive timeline still depends on X-energy successfully delivering its first power plant at a Dow Chemical plant southeast of Houston, Texas. The site, called Seadrift, has recently been at the center of a lawsuit filed by the state of Texas, which accuses the plant of “habitual non-compliance” with water and solid-waste regulations and permits.
X-energy has yet to break ground at Seadrift, which will host four Xe-100 reactors to provide the chemical plant with heat and electricity. The company said its construction permit is in the final phases of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s review process.
Startups and large cloud computing companies are betting that small modular reactors (SMRs), like the kind being developed by X-energy, will help pull the nuclear industry out of its slump. The most recent nuclear power plants built in the U.S. suffered from egregious budget overruns and slipped timelines.
By shrinking the reactor, companies like X-energy hope that mass manufacturing will keep costs and schedules in line. Even then, it could be a tall order. Experts say mass manufacturing often doesn’t start producing benefits for about a decade.
X-energy debuted on the Nasdaq in April in an IPO priced at $23 per share. Investor excitement drove the price up 27% in the first day of trading, but shares of the newly public company have dropped by nearly two-thirds since then.
News of the Amazon deal sent X-energy’s shares up about 10% in premarket trading, though they were down by less than 2% at the time of publication.

title_en: At what distance does a video doorbell stop detecting motion?
title_fa: At what distance does a video doorbell stop detecting motion?
excerpt_en: Your video doorbell might see a visitor without sending an alert. Detection depends on more than distance, and some surprising factors can affect its reach.
excerpt_fa: Your video doorbell might see a visitor without sending an alert. Detection depends on more than distance, and some surprising factors can affect its reach.
content_en:
At what distance does a video doorbell stop detecting motion?
Not all video doorbells are made equal.
Just because someone is seen by your video doorbell does not mean that the device will detect them and alert you. Ring says the standard maximum motion detection range for its devices is about 30 feet (9 meters), but if the object is much bigger than a person, such as a car passing by, it can still trigger an alert from farther away.
Still, maximum distances for these products aren't guaranteed. Some companies' video doorbells have much shorter published ranges than Ring, which we'll explore below, and capabilities can fall short of a maximum advertised range depending on a camera's sensitivity, mounting location and surroundings. Someone may be visible during live view, but not trigger a motion event because detection is based on more than what the camera can see. The sensor, camera angle, directional movement and software settings all factor in.
Motion detection range varies by video doorbell
According to eufy, its Video Doorbell can reliably detect horizontal motion up to 15 feet away and vertical motion up to 5 feet away. Arlo lists a maximum motion detection range of 13 feet for its second-generation Video Doorbell, while the Essential wired and wire-free models are listed at 16 feet. According to TELUS, the doorbell's motion sensor works best within 8 feet.
However, it's not just about distance. Even at its most sensitive setting, TELUS says its doorbell's motion sensor requires continuous movement for seven seconds or more to trigger a clip. Ring does not state a single per-model maximum for every current doorbell on its general motion settings page.
Motion detection type is equally as important. On one hand, you have passive infrared (PIR) heat sensors, which are more sensitive to side-to-side movement than motion directly toward or away from the camera. In contrast, Pixel Difference Analysis (PDA) compares one video frame with the next to identify differences. Popular examples of each include the Wyze Duo Cam Doorbell, which uses PIR, while Logitech's Circle View uses PDA. Some cameras, like SimpliSafe video doorbells, combine video analytics with PIR.
More motion range isn't always better
If a device like your 4K Ring doorbell isn't detecting visitors in time, you can adjust its Motion Sensitivity and its detection range up to the maximum limit. Companies like Ring also allow you to establish up to three customizable motion zones per device. Motion zones determine which areas of the camera's field of view should detect for recording motion events.
If your front door is on a busy road, that's an important distinction. Ring says that moving trees, sunlight, reflections and shadows can lead to unwanted alerts, and that large vehicles can trigger a motion alert even beyond a standard range, as we established.
There's a battery tradeoff, as well, for wireless or battery-powered doorbell cameras. Google says its battery-powered Nest Doorbell naturally consumes more power when detecting high-traffic areas like a busy sidewalk. In this event, the device's Activity Zones, or a different camera angle, can reduce unnecessary triggers. Ring recommends mounting its video doorbells 48 inches off the ground.
User experience may differ by subscription. Ring allows customers to receive and respond to motion alerts for free, but viewing recorded video requires a Ring Protect subscription, as do Smart Alerts distinguishing between people, vehicles and packages. The company doesn't say that paying for a subscription makes the physical motion detection range bigger.

title_en: Fiber vs. cable internet: What's the difference between them?
title_fa: Fiber vs. cable internet: What's the difference between them?
excerpt_en: Fiber internet is more modern than cable, but the older technology still works well for today's connection needs.
excerpt_fa: Fiber internet is more modern than cable, but the older technology still works well for today's connection needs.
content_en:
Fiber vs. cable internet: What's the difference between them?
They're both suitable options for today's internet needs, but the right one for you depends on availability and price.
For both internet speed and reliability, fiber-optic and cable connections beat alternatives like DSL and satellite connectivity. Fiber is capable of much faster speeds and better reliability, but cable wins in availability while still keeping speeds fast enough. Depending on what you do online, the differences in speed and latency could result in buffering video streams, slow downloads or jittery connections while gaming online.
Fiber-optic cables transmit information as light through thin strands of glass wrapped in protective layers of plastic. As for cable, data moves through electricity. Cut open a coaxial cable, and you'll find a copper core insulated with metal and plastic layers. While it's convenient for ISPs since it utilizes the same infrastructure used to deliver cable TV, relying on electricity to transfer information makes it prone to interference from extreme weather or moisture.
Much of the time, picking between fiber and cable comes down to whether fiber is available in your area. The Fiber Broadband Association found that over 60 percent of American households had access to fiber connectivity as of September 2025, while 96.9 percent of Americans have access to a fixed broadband service at 100/20 Mbps according to the FCC. If you have a choice, you should know how they differ and what makes the most sense for your home.
Is fiber or cable better for internet?
Fiber connections provide better performance than cable because they support vastly higher bandwidth. They aren't subject to cable's physical limitations, where available bandwidth has to be split between two "lanes" for uploading and downloading. For that reason, fiber is also more reliable than cable during peak usage hours. Cable networks share bandwidth with neighboring households, which is why you might notice slower speeds in the evenings when everyone is at home streaming.
While you might see fiber speeds start around 100 Mbps, it's more common to see entry-level offerings around 300 or 500 Mbps, with plans going much higher. As an example, Ziply Fiber offers plans from 2 Gbps all the way up to a wild 50 Gbps. Unlike cable, fiber internet is symmetrical, meaning the upload and download speeds are the same. If you often upload video, live stream or sync files, this is a big difference.
Many internet providers now opt for a hybrid fiber-coaxial network, where fiber lines connect a neighborhood before using coaxial cables for the final section to homes. While it may not be a true end-to-end fiber solution, you can still get download speeds of 1 Gbps or more this way, though upload speeds will be lower.
The cost of fiber compared to cable
A fiber subscription is not necessarily pricier than cable connectivity, depending on ISP deals and especially when you take upload speeds into account. Take Google Fiber, for example, where the 1 Gbps connection (both up and down) is $70 a month, 3 Gbps is $100/month and 8 Gbps is $150/month. In comparison, Xfinity's hybrid cable internet offers 300 Mbps down for $45/month, 500 Mbps down for $60/month, and 1 Gbps down for $70/month. Those prices are all locked in for five years (with no contract required) and will go up after the term.
For cable plans, you'll need to either use the ISP's all-in-one gateway or purchase your own modem and router separately. Fiber internet requires a dedicated Optical Network Terminal (ONT), a fiber equivalent to a modem which most service providers include with your plan.
In case you still want traditional cable or even a home phone, internet service providers often bundle TV services and phone lines with cable internet so you save more. Meanwhile, if you're not happy with the cable or fiber options available in your area, wireless 5G home internet is another potential route, though it's usually slower and has higher latency than wired solutions.
Regardless of which option you choose, you should know how to prevent your home network from running slowly. A cheap router or poorly optimized settings can result in slow Wi-Fi performance even if your ISP plan is super fast. Connecting with Ethernet sidesteps Wi-Fi's interference issues and reduces latency for real-time uses like gaming and video calls.

title_en: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
title_fa: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
excerpt_en: Fed up with ads, tracking, and sluggish interfaces, some smart TV owners are turning to AI agents to strip away bloatware and take back control of their TVs.
excerpt_fa: Fed up with ads, tracking, and sluggish interfaces, some smart TV owners are turning to AI agents to strip away bloatware and take back control of their TVs.
content_en:
The latest use case for AI? Dumbing down your smart TV to get rid of the bloat. A number of developers and vibe coders have recently been sharing solutions for “vibe-coding” your TV to get rid of sponsored ads, speed up the app launcher, redesign the home screen, disable tracking features, and more.
One such solution, called “dumbtv,” describes its mission on its GitHub page thus: “Your TV should do what you paid for: your apps, your HDMI inputs, and nothing else. No ads from the TV itself, no watch tracking, no update you did not ask for.”
Another, “cleanyourtv,” promises to strip the bloatware from any Android TV or Google TV over Wi-Fi, to replace the launcher with one that resembles Apple TV.
While hacking consumer electronics devices to gain more control over their systems is hardly a new idea, the latest advances in AI technology have made such efforts much more accessible to anyone. With smart TVs in particular, the hacks come at a time when people have grown frustrated with being forced to watch ads and put up with their devices surveilling their viewing habits.
Modern smart TVs ship with a technology called automatic content recognition (ACR), which identifies what’s playing on the screen using screenshots, audio clips, or other forms of digital fingerprinting.
If these “dumb TV” hacks become more popular among everyday consumers, they have the potential to disrupt the smart TV ad industry, which profits from selling viewing data to advertisers or using it to display personalized ads on their own interfaces.
As the creator of cleanyourtv, Gathin T., puts it, the idea to clean up the smart TV interface started one afternoon when he got tired of seeing the ads on his parents’ TV set.
“I had Claude Code clean it up over Wi-Fi and build a simple home screen with just their apps on it. I put the prompt on GitHub, tweeted the before and after, and a few thousand people did the same to their own TVs over the next two days. Xiaomi, TCL, Sony, Fire TV, LG, a projector or two,” the developer wrote on a website for donations, linked from the project’s homepage.
The solution doesn’t require gaining root access to the TV, nor does it make it impossible to return to the factory default state, if desired.
Meanwhile, the dumbtv solution has been tested end-to-end on a Fire TV Edition television set and Android/Google TV platforms on TVs from Sony, TCL, Philips, Hisense, Xiaomi, and Shield. To use this hack, the developer, Muzzammil Yasin Sabuwala, suggests pointing your preferred AI agent at the dumbtv repository on GitHub.
Sabuwala said he was motivated to work on dumbtv because he was tired of the ads and not being able to delve directly into the content he wanted to watch. His solution was coded using a combination of Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, he told TechCrunch, and he plans to maintain the GitHub, adding support for more models over time.
Fair warning: All these solutions are works in progress, and various users are now testing them across different TV platforms and suggesting updates and fixes.
However, individuals don’t need to borrow someone else’s work from GitHub to get the job done.
In one newly viral X post, Ryan Doyle explains that he simply sent Claude Code the listing for his TV and asked “Can you hack this?” The agent then talked him through the process, allowing him to remove the ads and bloatware from the TV set, speed up the lagging user interface, and customize his screensaver, he claims.
Doyle then goes on to demonstrate in a video how fast and responsive the new interface is after the AI made the requested changes.
Seeing posts about people “vibe-coding their TVs,” inspired one X user, Mihir Gupta, to try it himself.
“One afternoon with Claude Code: 25 bloat apps disabled, the 192 MB stock launcher replaced with a custom 83 MB one, plus rotating wallpapers,” he wrote.
The end result of these hacks may be mixed, however. Some people have found that Claude wouldn’t respond to their simple suggestions to “hack my TV,” necessitating more complex prompts. Others warned that AI agents could make mistakes, possibly disabling important packages or breaking things in the process. One person even said they bricked their Android TV using Claude, and another got stuck halfway through hacking their Fire TV.
For those wary of using AI to fully hack their TVs, there are existing solutions for customizing Android-based smart TVs, such as home screen replacement apps ATV Launcher, Projectivy Launcher, and FLauncher.
