title_en: TechCrunch Mobility: Rivian’s next act
title_fa: TechCrunch Mobility: Rivian’s next act
excerpt_en: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
excerpt_fa: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
content_en:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
As I wrapped my TechCrunch Disrupt interview with Rivian CEO and founder RJ Scaringe, I kept circling back to one question: What does Scaringe want Rivian to become? If you look at Rivian’s moves over the past year, it’s clear that Scaringe wants the company to be much more than an EV maker. But he doesn’t want to stray completely from that mission either.
Rivian is far more vertically integrated than it was just a couple of years ago. It has developed its own AI models to power its in-vehicle assistant and is building an end-to-end automated driving stack for its passenger vehicles and future robotaxis through a partnership with Uber. It’s even developing custom silicon, a 5 nm processor in collaboration with Arm and TSMC. And then there is its $5.8 billion joint technology venture with VW Group focused on electric architecture and software.
Scaringe’s ambitions extend beyond Rivian as well, although there is always a link back. He created a micromobility skunkworks program that has since spun out into a startup called Also. And he founded an industrial robotics startup called Mind Robotics, which is now 31% owned by Rivian and counts the automaker as a prospective customer. (Scaringe announced onstage that former Ford, Apple, and Tesla executive Doug Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics.)
Scaringe’s aspirations were on display as he talked of not only expanding the joint venture with VW to cover AI and autonomy, but also licensing Rivian’s tech to “many different brands.”
So what does Rivian look like at the end of the decade? Certainly not just a maker of electric trucks and SUVs. The term I kept coming back to was “tech supplier.”
Hear me out. Rivian is clearing a path toward licensing its electric architecture and software as well as its AI models and autonomy stack. Meanwhile, the Mind Robotics startup it partially owns is building industrial robots to not only be used in Rivian factories, but also sold to other companies. Then there’s the robotaxi business. A successful launch with Uber could open the door to more deals.
And Scaringe is already imagining how autonomy could reshape Rivian’s own vehicles.
“Where it gets really interesting is then you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities. It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.”
Deals!
Bedrock Robotics, a startup developing autonomous driving tech for construction vehicles, is raising $600 million, Axios reported, citing sources.
Dot Ai completed its acquisition of electric vehicle car-sharing business Envoy Technologies in a $65 million all-stock transaction, according to a regulatory filing.
Evos, a startup that developed AI agents to automate work for industrial businesses, including freight brokerages, raised $9 million in a pre-seed round co-led by Uncork Capital and Field Ventures.
Mana Battery, a Colorado-based startup developing anode-free sodium batteries, raised $10.15 million in a round led by Voyager Ventures.
PlusAI, the autonomous trucking developer, and Texas Ventures Acquisition III filed a Form S-4 registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission —advancing its previously announced agreement to go public via a merger with a blank-check company.
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. Neither company shared financial terms of the deal. The automaker plans to use a trio of Nvidia products to be able to offer hands-free, point-to-point driving on highways and surface streets.
Waabi, a startup developing self-driving trucks, landed a commercial partnership with carrier Warrior Logistics. Under the deal, Waabi’s self-driving trucks will move freight between Dallas and Houston.
Notable reads and other tidbits
Electric vehicle sales in the United States are showing signs of life.
Laplace Intelligence, one of 20 startups that competed in TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200, is building automated red-teaming that stress-tests robots and self-driving cars.
MIT startup LNK Energies says it has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from price spikes.
The Paris Auto Show puts Chinese cars on center stage.
Tesla showcased its SpaceX-powered Roadster with a theatrical kickflip stunt. The Roadster used a mix of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and stick a landing on the pavement below. CEO Elon Musk claims the vehicle will be on the road by 2028. But will future owners be allowed to legally deploy these maneuvers on public streets? I don’t see how.
Waymo is expanding into Canada — specifically, Toronto — after receiving approval to participate in an automated vehicle pilot program. Waymo has also opened up its robotaxi service to everyone, meaning no more waitlists, in San Antonio, San Diego, and Tampa.
One more thing …
TechCrunch reporter Tim De Chant recently test drove the 2026Porsche Macan Turbo EV. His week with the EV has him questioning what a sports car is supposed to be. Read the full review.

title_en: Flat Ethernet cables probably aren't the answer to your home networking problem
title_fa: Flat Ethernet cables probably aren't the answer to your home networking problem
excerpt_en: For the most reliable performance, round Ethernet cables are generally superior.
excerpt_fa: For the most reliable performance, round Ethernet cables are generally superior.
content_en:
Flat Ethernet cables probably aren't the answer to your home networking problem
For the most reliable performance, round cables are generally superior.
Unless you're relying entirely on Wi-Fi, chances are you've had to wrangle an unsightly mess of Ethernet cables at some point in your life. One way to make your home internet setup a little easier on the eyes is to use flat Ethernet cables, which have become much more popular in recent years. Flat Ethernet cables can be easily bent and hidden from sight, making it possible to wire a home for internet without causing an eyesore.
But before you trade out all your chunky old Ethernet cables for aesthetic flat ones, there are a few tradeoffs you should be aware of that might not be obvious at first. While round and flat Ethernet cables rated for the same speed will have nearly identical performance under perfect conditions, the real world is full of complications that often make round cables a better choice even if they don't look quite as good. It all comes down to why Ethernet cables are round in the first place and what it takes to turn them into that more pleasing flat shape.
Does a flat Ethernet cable affect speed?
Standard Ethernet cables consist of multiple sets of wires twisted into pairs, with each pair then twisted around each other. The twisting actually serves an important purpose, preventing the signal running through one pair of wires from interfering with the others, which could cause slow internet speeds and unstable connections. Flat Ethernet cables still contain twisted pairs of wires, but those pairs are laid out in a line, which makes them more susceptible to interference from each other. Some round Ethernet cables include additional shielding to prevent interference from outside devices, which typically isn't available in flat cables.
Another potential problem comes from the gauge, or thickness, of the wires inside Ethernet cables. To ensure that flat cables are as thin as possible, manufacturers typically use a thinner gauge wire than is used in round cables. The thinner a wire is, the more resistance the electricity traveling through it faces, meaning flat Ethernet cables can actually degrade signals over a long enough distance.
While the technical specifications of Ethernet make flat cables a dicey choice, the real problem comes from how they tend to be used. Flat Ethernet cables are easy to bend around corners, run under doors, and hide beneath rugs, but all of these applications make them much more likely to fail. Bending any cable or repeatedly compressing it under a door can end up damaging the wires within, no matter what shape it's in. The thinner wires in flat Ethernet cables make them more fragile, and since they're laid out in a row, they lack even the slight cushioning that the shape of round cables can offer.
Are flat Ethernet cables any good?
While there are real drawbacks to using flat Ethernet cables, that doesn't necessarily mean that they should be avoided at all costs, and there are some circumstances where using them makes a lot of sense in a home setup. If you absolutely need to run a cable under a door or through another space too narrow to fit a round cable, using a flat cable may be your only option, especially if you're renting and can't make big changes to your living space. It may also be worth the risk to use flat cables you can hide under rugs if the alternative is turning your office into a rat's nest of visible wires.
If you absolutely need the fastest, most reliable connection, round Ethernet cables are almost always going to be the best choice. Where that's not necessary or possible, though, flat cables can work fine as long as you know their limitations. One way to make your home internet setup a little easier on the eyes is to use flat Ethernet cables, which have become much more popular in recent years. Flat Ethernet cables can be easily bent and hidden from sight, making it possible to wire a home for internet without causing an eyesore.

Standard Ethernet cables consist of multiple sets of wires twisted into pairs, with each pair then twisted around each other. title_en: The reason why your drive shows less storage than you paid for
title_fa: The reason why your drive shows less storage than you paid for
excerpt_en: Despite showing the storage amount on the box or the spec sheet, your new device might not actually hold as much as it states. Here are the reasons why.
excerpt_fa: Despite showing the storage amount on the box or the spec sheet, your new device might not actually hold as much as it states. Here are the reasons why.
content_en:
The reason why your drive shows less storage than you paid for
Understanding the difference between decimal and binary.
Device storage is extremely valuable these days. The rabid appetite of AI datacenters is inflating drive pricing so badly that companies like Apple and Valve have jacked up the prices of some products by hundreds of dollars. Even if that wasn't happening, though, the size of apps, media and operating systems is continually growing, filling up the storage we do have. Some PC and console games can top 100GB, especially if they're live service titles with a lot of downloadable content.
All this is to say that if there's a gap between the amount of storage you're promised for an internal or external drive versus what's actually usable, the disappointment may be palpable now more than ever. Recently, for example, we discovered that a 512GB drive only registered as offering 477GB accessible to Windows. On paper, that 35GB difference might be enough to fit someone's entire photo library, or maybe a converted 4K HDR movie.
In most instances, the root of these discrepancies boils down to how different companies calculate data, rather than a naked attempt to rip you off. At other times, it may be a matter of a device being unusable without some of that space going to pre-installed software.
The harsh impacts of math
Frequently, storage makers calculate storage capacity using a base-10 (decimal) system. In that arrangement, a kilobyte is 1,000 bytes, a gigabyte is 1 billion bytes, and so forth. And that probably makes sense to you, given how measurements work in most other areas of life, especially if you live in a country using the metric system for weights and distances. It's a lot easier to market to the average consumer.
The thing is, software platforms like Windows often gauge capacity in binary terms. That transforms a kilobyte into 1,024 bytes, and a gigabyte into 1,073,741,824 bytes. As figures get larger, the gap between binary and decimal calculations becomes vast. A 1TB drive may show as holding just 931GB in Windows, despite nothing actually being lost. You will see the full 1TB available on a Mac, where decimal reigns supreme.
This is obviously problematic if you're expecting storage marketed in binary terms versus the way hardware makers label it. To our knowledge, Microsoft doesn't have any intention of switching Windows from binary to decimal, and Apple isn't planning to revert the Mac, iPad, iPhone or other products back to binary. You can expect this inconsistency to exist in the market for a while longer.
There have been attempts to make the situation clearer by using binary-specific terms such as "kibibyte" (KiB) and "gibibyte" (GiB). As you've probably noticed, though, these haven't caught on, even within binary-based platforms. If you check the file size of something in Windows 11, you'll see KB or GB instead.
The operating system complication
A complaint you'll run into occasionally is that the new phone, tablet, laptop or console they bought doesn't have as much usable space as they expected. This can potentially be linked to the binary-decimal split we just talked about, but the bigger culprit tends to be the device OS, which has to be pre-installed for anything to work. iOS 27 consumes over 22GB (decimal) on a 128GB iPhone 16 Pro, and on one of our gaming laptops, Windows 11 occupies over 81GB (binary). It's no wonder that 64GB devices are effectively extinct, and that even 128GB is becoming impractical.
As if things weren't complicated enough, operating systems tend to grow every year as new features are added. And to run smoothly, most devices need additional cache and swap space for temporary files. This space isn't necessarily marked off-limits. If it isn't, though, you can accidentally harm performance by downloading too many files or installing too many apps. Vanishing swap space bogs down performance, and can lead to apps crashing or freezing.
To cope with this unfortunate scenario, all you can really do is be conservative with your usage and shopping habits. If you avoid waste and overestimate the amount of storage you need, even a few dozen gigabytes can be an acceptable sacrifice. Don't panic if you notice this when planning your next electronics haul.

The Legion Go S with SteamOS is a pretty solid alternative to the $789 Steam Deck OLED. It runs identical software, but ships in a design with two-stage triggers, a bigger eight-inch IPS screen (1080p and up to 120Hz versus 800p and 90Hz in the Deck OLED), and it’s got double the RAM and storage (32GB and 1TB, respectively), not to mention a slightly faster processor in the Ryzen Z1 Extreme.
Lenovo’s fast, comfy SteamOS handheld is hundreds off
With double the RAM and storage of the base Steam Deck OLED, plus a slightly faster processor, this is a great deal.
With double the RAM and storage of the base Steam Deck OLED, plus a slightly faster processor, this is a great deal.
At $999.99, its current discounted price at Best Buy, it’s worth considering if you’re deciding on a handheld. The Legion Go S is not as powerful as the $1,299.99 Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 that just launched, which has the Z2 Extreme and a OLED screen, but it’s no slouch, either.
This model launched with Windows 11 and the Ryzen Z2 Go. Despite being a newer chip, it’s less powerful than the Z1 Extreme in the discounted model. SteamOS and the faster internals within this configuration will provide a better experience. Check out my colleague Sean Hollister’s review of multiple configs of the Go S, and see how it stacks up in his benchmarks.

title_en: iOS 27's new CarPlay features are great, but only these iPhones can actually use them
title_fa: iOS 27's new CarPlay features are great, but only these iPhones can actually use them
excerpt_en: With the release of iOS 27, car owners with CarPlay support can enjoy lots of cool new features. However, not all iPhone models are able to support them all.
excerpt_fa: With the release of iOS 27, car owners with CarPlay support can enjoy lots of cool new features. However, not all iPhone models are able to support them all.
content_en:
iOS 27's new CarPlay features are great, but only these iPhones can actually use them
If your iPhone is less than three years old, you're in luck.
Apple's iOS 27 update doesn't just bring new features for iPhone users — it also adds a bunch of new options to CarPlay for a better in-car experience. The upgrades aren't huge, but they definitely make CarPlay easier and more enjoyable to use.
For starters, the Now Playing screen has finally got a progress bar and a persistent mini-player, while navigation apps can share route data with the car. There are also new wallpapers, performance improvements and the long-awaited Siri AI right inside your vehicle. But there's a catch: these features require an iPhone running iOS 27, and even if you have one, you might need one of the newer models to unlock all of what's possible.
What's new in CarPlay with iOS 27
A major upgrade to CarPlay with iOS 27 is support for video apps. Until now, CarPlay's entertainment support was limited to audio services like Apple Music and Spotify, but drivers can now watch videos on their vehicle's display.
That doesn't mean you can watch a movie while driving, though. The feature detects when the car is in motion and, for safety reasons, only becomes available once the vehicle is parked. If you're watching something and start driving, playback automatically switches to audio-only until you come to a stop. Still, it's a nice option to have. One thing to keep in mind is that vehicle manufacturers need to implement support for this new feature, which might mean apps like YouTube or Netflix might not work inside your car right now.
Audio playback has also improved, with Now Playing having a mini-player that includes the album artwork, playback controls and a long-awaited progress bar. Just swipe to skip forward or backward through a song or podcast without having to reach for your iPhone. Speaking of improvements, Apple claims that CarPlay has become much more reliable in iOS 27. Not only can you expect a more consistent wireless connection, but also more accurate GPS location reporting.
There are also new wallpapers to choose from and the ability for apps to share route data with your vehicle to include information such as EV charging stops. This allows your vehicle to cross-check arrival times with Google Maps and Apple Maps and suggest locations to juice up along the route.
Siri AI is here too, but only if you have the right iPhone
Siri AI, the updated version of Apple's virtual assistant, is also available in CarPlay with iOS 27. It works pretty much the same way as it does on other Apple devices — it can answer general knowledge questions or even use personal context to find answers in your emails, messages and calendar. For example, you can ask Siri to get directions to a restaurant that someone recommended to you during a conversation. You can also use more natural language to search for directions in Apple Maps — like asking Siri to avoid tolls on your route.
You can only take advantage of these features if you have an iPhone compatible with Siri AI. That means an iPhone 15 Pro or an iPhone 16 or later. Since CarPlay runs entirely on your iPhone, an older iPhone doesn't have the hardware required to power Siri AI in your car. An iPhone 14 owner, for example, still gets the mini-player, the progress bar and the new wallpapers, but not the new Siri experience.
Still, you'll need to update your iPhone to iOS 27 first. The update is available for the iPhone 11 and later, so if you have an older iPhone, you're out of luck. Your CarPlay will continue to operate, just with the features it already supports.
Siri AI also isn't available in the European Union due to local regulations, so that's something to keep in mind. If you live in Europe and own a compatible iPhone, you'll still get the new CarPlay features, but not Siri AI.
If you've already prepared and updated your iPhone to iOS 27, it's worth checking out a few settings that can help improve your CarPlay experience.

title_en: The reason your Amazon Alexa devices are always listening
title_fa: The reason your Amazon Alexa devices are always listening
excerpt_en: Alexa devices have microphones that are always listening, but what does Amazon do with that data? It's up to you.
excerpt_fa: Alexa devices have microphones that are always listening, but what does Amazon do with that data? It's up to you.
content_en:
The reason your Amazon Alexa devices are always listening
It's not as nefarious as it sounds.
Amazon Alexa in all its forms has become increasingly prevalent across households — over 600 million Alexa-enabled devices have been purchased worldwide since its initial release. Even though this doesn't translate directly to active Alexa users, it's still an impressive figure that, for many people, conjures up privacy concerns. This proliferation of Alexa is only going to increase, with Amazon just announcing several new products, many of which — like the company's new line of tablets — actively involve Alexa.
Willingly placing a microphone-centric device in your home certainly sounds very Big Brother-esque, especially with how quickly you can build an entire Alexa ecosystem to essentially run every device in the house. This integration is even more compounded with the continued rollout of Alexa+, which is designed to have additional real-world applications. But is Alexa really always eavesdropping on everything you say? It depends on how you define listening.
Why your Alexa is always listening
In a technical sense, your Alexa isn't listening verbatim to every word you say around it, at least according to Amazon. Instead, it's listening for "acoustic patterns" that match its particular wake word. It's sort of like listening to a conversation with earplugs in — you can't hear the exact words being said, but you'd still likely recognize someone saying your name because it's a sound pattern you've heard many times before. Once Alexa recognizes its wake word, it will switch over to active listening to respond to your request, and only then will it record any audio or send it to the cloud.
This is the best balance Amazon has been able to find between privacy and what Alexa needs to serve its main purpose, i.e., conversational assistance. If the device isn't listening on some level, there's no way for it to know you're asking it something. On the bright side, Alexa devices are designed to record as little audio as possible, only saving direct conversations you have with the device, and there are ways to adjust Alexa to further assuage privacy concerns.
How to improve privacy with Alexa
Of course, the most straightforward way to eliminate any eavesdropping Alexa concerns is to simply mute your device's microphone. For most Alexa devices made by Amazon (the Echo lineup), the button to do so is located on the top of the device and looks like a microphone with a slash through it. Once you press it, you'll know the microphone is muted by the red light displayed on the Echo device. It's a bit antithetical to how the device is designed to be used, but if you don't mind manually turning the microphone on and off each time you want to ask Alexa something, it's an easy fix for privacy concerns.
If you still want to be able to call out to Alexa without fiddling with a button each time, you can adjust your recording settings for extra data protection. To do so:
-
Open the Alexa app.
-
Tap the three lines, then select Alexa Privacy.
-
Select Manage Your Alexa Data.
-
Select Voice Recordings and Transcripts.
From here, you'll have four options: saving them for three or 18 months, saving until you delete them or not retaining them at all. On the Alexa data screen, you can also toggle how other data is saved (or not), like smart home device and detected sounds histories. With some devices, you can also toggle on this screen whether to allow deletion by voice, so that you can say things like, "Alexa, delete everything I said today," or, "Delete my entire voice history." However, this doesn't work with devices running Alexa+ or Amazon Kids.
Keep in mind that these settings only work for the Amazon cloud itself. If you use Alexa with third-party devices like robotic vacuums or smart TVs, those companies may still have access to your history after deletion. Deleting your voice recordings can also impact how well Alexa is able to personalize its responses to you, as it makes the device unable to maintain a voice profile for you — if that doesn't bother you, then delete away.

content_en:
Dinosaur Jr. frontman J Mascis is known as something of a slacker guitar god. He stands stoically onstage, barely moving, as he seemingly effortlessly works through deft guitar solos and lopsided riffs. Unfortunately, Mascis has developed a similar reputation as an interview subject, quietly sitting and offering deft nonanswers.
J Mascis has nothing better to do

That’s not to say that Mascis can’t be funny or charming. As our interview was winding down and I was thanking him for his time, he started to loosen up a bit. He told me about his youth as a mini golf “enthusiast.” “I had a 3-foot putt for the win” at a mini-golf tournament, he said, but “that’s when I realized that I was a choker … When I was 11, I choked.” And that’s when he decided, “I should maybe not do sports.” So, instead of becoming a professional mini golfer, Mascis went on to form one of the most important bands in alternative rock.
While most of his contemporaries have called it quits or are just going through the motions onstage for a paycheck, the original lineup of Mascis, bassist Lou Barlow, and drummer Patrick Murphy are still regularly putting out new LPs of reliable rockers. But Mascis says there isn’t any grand secret to the band’s longevity. Over 40 years deep, he says, “I guess we have nothing better to do.”
What, for an interviewer, can come off as frustrating indifference might actually be the key to Mascis’ staying power — for better or worse. Creatively and professionally, his modus operandi seems to be rolling with the punches and not overthinking things.
For the new record There Near, he said, the band “just didn’t push it.” There were no eight-hour marathon studio sessions. They weren’t meticulously fine-tuning basslines or trading Logic sessions back and forth remotely. Mascis would roll in with fully prepared demos and the band would immediately start recording, even as Barlow and Murph were still learning their parts, “on the off chance that it comes together quickly.”
The same sort of relaxed approach also informs Mascis’ gear choices. He said, “I am kind of a tube purist guy, but it’s just also kind of inconvenient sometimes,” so he uses whatever works. That means while he mixes and masters to tape, he’s also tracking in Pro Tools.
When it comes to designing signature instruments with Fender, he’s just as easygoing. “I try to, you know, do the important things that I want, but not make it too complicated … I think it’s better to keep it kind of cheap … just so people can do what they want with it.” The neck is his biggest concern, he said. “I’m a sucker for jumbo frets and, you know, if the neck is good and the frets and stuff, that’s the main thing. Most of the other stuff, you know, you can swap out if you want.”
But that somewhat lackadaisical attitude has also caught him some heat. Two years ago, Mascis released a video for his solo track “Old Friends” that was made using generative AI. Speaking with The Verge, he finally publicly addressed the controversy. “Yeah, just some kid did it,” he said. “I thought it looked cool, so… Yeah, that’s dipping my toes into the... I don’t do much with videos.” He trailed off repeatedly while answering before finally admitting, “But yeah, I guess that’s a slippery slope.”
Similarly, he said that while he doesn’t believe there is a place for AI in music making, we have to acknowledge that it’s here whether we like it or not, and “I guess we’re learning how to deal with it. And hopefully it won’t kill us all.”
About the only thing that Mascis could muster strong feelings about was the band’s infamously loud live shows. (Dinosaur Jr.’s recent performance at the tiny Baby’s All Right is what finally convinced me to start packing earplugs.) “I noticed the audience too seems more desperate for something kind of reality-based,” he said, letting a touch of his purist heart show. “We don’t have in-ear monitors or click tracks. We have amps and you know, just, I think some people are responding to the reality of it. Like they really need something that’s not, you know, computer-generated or something.”
He bemoaned the lack of amps onstage (Mascis plays in front of three full stacks, even in a 280-person-capacity club) and the reliance on high-tech front-of-house setups. “It’s very weird. Now, soundmen create the sound instead of capture the sound,” he said. Of course, his recognition of the visceral power of live music and directly connecting with an audience makes his indifference to AI all the more baffling.
Dinosaur Jr. are currently touring the US behind There Near, which is out now.

title_en: These 6 retro sites let you relive the glory days of 2000s Flash games
title_fa: These 6 retro sites let you relive the glory days of 2000s Flash games
excerpt_en: Flash hasn't been around for over half a decade, but thanks to archivists, you can still enjoy this era of the internet.
excerpt_fa: Flash hasn't been around for over half a decade, but thanks to archivists, you can still enjoy this era of the internet.
content_en:
These 6 retro sites let you relive the glory days of 2000s Flash games
You can still enjoy Flash classics long after the old plugin's demise.
Browser-based Flash games hark back to a simpler time on the internet: the days of Neopets, Homestar Runner, MySpace and AOL Instant Messenger. Many millennials and others who were online in this era carry intense feelings of nostalgia for Flash and the online media it enabled. In a post titled Why Preserve Flash?, internet archivist Jason Scott wrote, "Flash flew across the mid-2000s internet sky in a blaze of glory and unbridled creativity. It was the backbone of menus and programs and even critical applications for working with sites."
Adobe ended support for Flash Player on December 31, 2020. This was due to a changing landscape where standards like HTML5 reduced the need for plugins like Flash, which suffered from security vulnerabilities that couldn't be sufficiently addressed over the years. The demise of this browser plugin put thousands of pieces of early internet memorabilia at risk of disappearing. Flash not only powered web-based games, but also early video streaming including YouTube, Hulu and seasons of shows like My Little Pony.
But that doesn't mean content built with Flash is gone forever. You can thankfully still play Flash games in 2026 using websites that run the original programs, most of them using an open-source Flash emulator called Ruffle.
1. Flash Museum
The Flash Museum is a digital preservation project dedicated to archiving iconic Flash games and animations. Thanks to Ruffle, its Flash games are playable in modern browsers without the security risks of the original software. It hosts a massive library containing over 100,000 Flash games and more than 20,000 Flash animations across dozens of genres.
Anyone who was online in the 2000s probably remembers classic animations like Salad Fingers, Charlie the Unicorn and Badger Badger Badger — these and many more are available on the site. It also hosts beloved games from the era including Kingdom Rush, Tanks and Meat Boy.
Wondering where to start? Try Happy Wheels, a side-scrolling obstacle course with ragdoll physics and gore, where hitting obstacles can make your character suffer a gruesome fate. It was originally released in 2010 and is considered a classic Flash game.
2. Newgrounds
While not exclusively dedicated to preserving Flash games, entertainment website Newgrounds remains one of the most influential websites in the history of user-generated games and art, and still has a number of Flash games playable on its site. Historically, its community would vote on new uploads to the site to remove low-quality submissions.
Under that system, a number of famous franchises got their start as Flash games on the site, including Super Meat Boy. The game Castle Crashers was also started by developers involved with Newgrounds. Other well-loved animations of the time were first published here, including Salad Fingers and Charlie the Unicorn. The site has playlists dedicated to classic Flash games, including Stick RPG, a wildly popular title that plays like Grand Theft Auto in a stripped-down 2D format.
Newgrounds still accepts new publications today, so you can enjoy new submissions alongside the classics.
3. Kongregate
Kongregate is not entirely dedicated to Flash game archival, but offers many games of that era for nostalgic revisiting. For a classic Flash experience, consider playing its archived version of Bloons, a single-player puzzle game first developed in Flash and released in 2007. The original was simple: use a dart to pop a certain number of balloons in as few shots as possible. Since then, it has morphed into a massive franchise across PC, mobile, and even Netflix.
Shortly before the demise of Flash, Kongregate stopped accepting new game submissions, freezing its massive collection (more than 120,000 titles). However, it has since expanded into mobile game publishing, and in April 2026, the site announced it would again accept new games.
4. Armor Games
Like Newgrounds and Kongregate, Armor Games was a popular platform for publishing independent games in the 2000s. Unlike its competitors that allowed anyone to upload their creations, Armor Games hand-picked titles and invited certain developers to its curated collection. It was known for more family-friendly and polished games, rather than the edgy, occasionally PG-13 vibe of Newgrounds. Armor Games was the launching pad for some huge hits, including Kingdom Rush.
Today, it holds over 3,700 Flash games in its archive, including Warfare 1917 and Crush the Castle. Armor has also migrated a number of legacy Flash games to its storefront on Steam.
5. Flashpoint Archive
Flashpoint Archive is the most comprehensive repository of Flash games available online, though it requires a little more setup than the above. The platform was launched in 2017 after Adobe announced the end of Flash, intending to preserve this slice of internet culture. Today, it hosts a massive collection of more than 150,000 Flash-based games and animations.
Instead of running them on a website, Flashpoint Archive hosts the games for you to download and run on your own device, enabling you to play complex titles closer to their original forms. It has two options: Flashpoint Infinity is a small download where you choose which games to download as you go, while Flashpoint Ultimate is over 2TB and includes every game in one package.
Among its hundreds of thousands of titles, it hosts games like Dad 'n Me — a 2D brawler first released on Newgrounds in 2005.
6. The Internet Archive
The mission of the Internet Archive is to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge" by creating a free, public digital library that preserves webpages and other physical or digital archives over time. It's thus no surprise that when Flash was on its way out, archive enthusiasts jumped into action.
Unlike Flashpoint Archive, the Internet Archive sought to maintain the original...

title_en: Trump says Google kisses his ass

excerpt_en: During a rally on Saturday, October 17th, in Highland Heights, Kentucky, Donald Trump bragged about how much more powerful and influential he was during his second term. While listing off his accomplishments, he mentioned his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake...

content_en:
During a rally on Saturday, October 17th, in Highland Heights, Kentucky, Donald Trump bragged about how much more powerful and influential he was during his second term. While listing off his accomplishments, he mentioned his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario.
Trump says Google kisses his ass
Trump bragged at a rally that ‘Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first term. Now they kiss my ass.‘
Trump bragged at a rally that ‘Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first term. Now they kiss my ass.‘
“This is a much more powerful term. I can do stuff that’s unbelievable … I called Google, Google Maps. See, Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first term. Now they kiss my ass.”
Trump seems to be implying that he convinced Google to reflect the name change personally. That would seem to contradict Google’s statement on the matter, in which it said that it simply reflects “official government sources, which is GNIS for the US … These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”
Throughout his second term, however, Silicon Valley — including Google and its CEO Sundar Pichai — has gone out of its way to try and ingratiate itself with President Trump, lavishing him with gifts, compliments, and donations to his pet projects. Google did not immediately return a request for comment.

content_en:
Back in February, I went to Los Angeles to take in some art and stayed in Koreatown. Down the street from my hotel, there was this little coffee shop — Stagger — that is, I think, best known for its matcha, which is good. But the drink I unexpectedly found myself obsessed with was their cream top, an iced Americano with, yep, vanilla cream on top. When I got back to Oakland, I kept thinking about how badly I wanted one.
The best gadget I bought this year is a milk frother
Let me convince you to change up your coffee game.
Let me convince you to change up your coffee game.
For more than 20 years, I’ve been drinking my coffee — iced or otherwise — black. Originally this was because I knew I could put black coffee that had cooled off in the microwave to reheat it without worrying that the milk in it would curdle. (Gross, I know.) Then, as I started drinking better coffee, it felt like the best way to appreciate the expensive beans I was buying.
So my attachment to the cream top surprised me. And then, when Oakland had a gnarly heat wave in March, I decided there was one way I’d tolerate it: fancy coffee drinks. I splashed out $14 for the Zulay Kitchen frother and I was off.
A handheld foamer looks and works kinda like an immersion blender. I pour milk into a glass, stick the frother in there, and then hold the power button until it reaches my preferred consistency. When the disposable batteries it uses are fresh, this takes about 30 seconds to a minute. As the batteries degrade, it takes longer; if I’m getting impatient about how long it’s taking me to make my frothy treats, it’s time to change the batteries. The frother also works to beat eggs, mix protein powder or creatine into a drink, and make hot chocolate. But by far it’s gotten the most use making my coffee drinks as I set out to make a cream top of my own.
The cream top descended from the Einspänner, an espresso drink that’s named for a one-horse carriage. The original Viennese version used hot espresso, and the whipped cream on top served as a kind of insulation, which kept the drivers’ drinks hot for them when they were out in the cold. (Obviously, its popularity expanded beyond carriage drivers.) It isn’t clear to me how the Einspänner made it to South Korea, but it exploded in popularity there, with all kinds of variations, mostly iced. And then from South Korea, it made its way to the US, where the ground had already been cleared by Starbucks’ “cold foam” drinks.
The notable thing about the cream top, besides the addition of delicious fat and sugar to coffee, was that the cream wasn’t as light as latte foam, but wasn’t as heavy as ordinary whipped cream. It was melty and dripped slowly into the coffee.
My first experiments with my at-home cream top were pretty simple. I don’t have an espresso machine, but I do make concentrated cold brew in hot weather, which has a strong enough flavor to stand up against the foam. (Some recipes suggest powdered espresso if you don’t want to use concentrated cold brew.)
After I mastered the simple cream top, I began making forays into weirder breakfast treats, my favorite of which I… recreated from a Starbucks ad. It’s a cold brew with coconut ube cold foam, the top of which I dust with toasted coconut flakes. It is dank. (This is a recipe for a more sophisticated version than I make.) So when it was 90 degrees in Oakland for about two weeks running recently, this drink was how I consoled myself.
To be honest, I’m just recommending getting a frother. You can spend a lot on a milk frother and some people do. I relied on America’s Test Kitchen to steer me in the right direction — but outlets like Wirecutter and Bon Appétit have their own preferred options. This one is cheap and simple, and it’s been treating me right. I’m sure the Apple HomeView is nice, too, but in pleasure per dollar can it match a $14 cold foamer that takes AA batteries? I have my doubts.

But then came a bit of technology, previously mostly used for military purposes, called the overhead projector. It would change far more than just the disciplinary record of students everywhere.
How overhead projectors took over your classroom
On Version History: How a bit of military tech changed the way we learn forever.
On Version History: How a bit of military tech changed the way we learn forever.
In this episode of Version History, we tell the story of the overhead projector. David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Jake Kastrenakes and Stanford professor Antero Garcia to discuss how overhead projectors were developed, how they made their way into classrooms, and how they changed so much about the way kids learn. They also try to figure out why overhead projectors have mostly gone away, and whether the things that replaced them — from PowerPoint presentations to computer screens to those new-fangled smart boards — actually improved on the OHP.
This is the final episode of the fifth season of Version History, all about the most iconic school tech. Thanks so much for watching, listening, sending feedback, and everything else! Other than the OHP, we also spent this season looking at Oregon Trail, the original Chromebook, the One Laptop Per Child program, the LeapFrog LeapPad, and those ubiquitous Texas Instruments calculators. If you missed any part of our season, check out the episodes here:

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
How it started
The first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged.
Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars.
While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road.
The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators.
How it’s going
Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos.
Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle. They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations.
It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines. It used to be the case that Republicans were seen as more welcoming of autonomous vehicles, while Democrats were seen as more skeptical. This has certainly borne out in a handful of Democrat-led cities — New York City, Chicago, Washington, DC — that still haven’t legalized driverless cars. But now even some red states are considering tightening the leash, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa.
Even in tech-friendly California, state lawmakers are mulling ways to bring robotaxis to heel. Several bills have been introduced to give cities direct authority to limit AV fleet sizes, restrict operating hours, or enact local permit bans within municipal limits. Additionally, emergency protocols were drafted to require AV companies to give local police and fire departments physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms.
Some municipalities are flexing their land-use and zoning powers to crack down on robot cars. Culver City explored emergency moratoriums on building permits for AV fleet facilities, while Santa Monica used local noise and traffic ordinances to restrict 24-hour charging hubs. It would seem that even robotaxis aren’t immune to NIMBY complaints.
What happens next
As the local debate over autonomous vehicles intensifies, AV developers are increasingly looking overseas as a potential hedge to more obstacles in cropping up in the US. Waymo is planning to expand its service in London, Tokyo, and Munich. Uber is teeing up vehicles for Manchester, Madrid, and Dubai. If the US is getting too complex and over-regulated, perhaps they can find friendlier reception elsewhere.
Still, the US presents the industry’s best chances of turning a profit, especially as costs for developers continue to grow. Rather than fighting strict local regulations head-on, companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Aurora are prioritizing states with explicit legislative preemption that prevents individual cities from banning the technology. And at the national level, industry trade groups like the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association are aggressively pushing for more preemption powers in an attempt to create more unified standards.
Congress may eventually get around to passing high-level safety legislation, but it’s highly unlikely that any bill passed at the federal level would seek to strip...

title_en: You don't have to turn off your phone to switch SIM cards (but you probably should)
title_fa: You don't have to turn off your phone to switch SIM cards (but you probably should)
excerpt_en: Swapping SIM cards isn't something you'll do all the time, but when it does come up, you should do it carefully.
excerpt_fa: Swapping SIM cards isn't something you'll do all the time, but when it does come up, you should do it carefully.
content_en:
You don't have to turn off your phone to switch SIM cards (but you probably should)
A quick step removes the small chance of anything going wrong and requiring more of your time.
If your phone has a SIM tray, it's not something you likely open often, but there are still reasons to. You may be switching to an MVNO to save money, or maybe you're temporarily swapping out your normal SIM for a cheaper local carrier when travelling. In some cases, your carrier will send you a replacement card if yours is damaged.
Most of today's smartphones let you switch SIMs with the phone on, so you don't need to switch your device off for the process. But there are modest benefits if you do, and for something so quick, it's better to be safe if you have a few minutes.
How to replace the SIM
We're talking about physical SIM cards, which you have to remove from your phone by hand. eSIM replacement should be as simple as using a QR code, carrier app or direct transfer between different smartphones. Most eSIM-compatible phones can store many eSIMS, though only a few can be active at once.
Physical SIM card replacement involves these steps:
- Optionally, power down your phone or enable airplane mode.
- Pop the tray out, usually by gently pushing a paperclip or SIM ejector tool into the ejection pinhole on the phone.
- Change the card, ensuring you use the correct card size.
- Pop the tray back into place.
- Enter your PIN or restart if the phone requests it.
If you have a dual-SIM phone that supports two physical cards, check which SIM you intend to swap before you begin.
While many argue eSIM is a superior technology because it requires no moving parts, others still appreciate the convenience and relative privacy true SIM cards provide. They make it easy to install and use over-the-counter pay-as-you-go SIM-based accounts, for example.
The small potential risks of SIM replacement
Most potential dangers of SIM replacement are physical. You might accidentally insert dirt, grime or moisture into the SIM tray, or force a larger card into a smaller slot incorrectly. You could also break the SIM tray so it no longer aligns correctly, or otherwise harm the card. A damaged SIM card or one incorrectly inserted may cause the phone to continue trying (and failing) to create a network connection, draining its battery and causing it to overheat.
Most people never encounter these problems, since slowing down and being careful does the trick. In most cases, your phone will take a moment to read the new SIM and find the network. Then it will be available for service, subject to account setup requirements.
The benefit of turning your phone off before swapping the SIM is minor. It forces your phone to look at the fresh information provided on the new card when it powers on again, helping register your device on its new network more quickly by reading the new carrier settings. This reduces the chance you'll encounter a software-based "network error" message when you swap.
More to think about when swapping SIMs
Before the 2010s, SIM slots were usually located underneath a phone's removable battery, which obviously required powering off the device to access. Over time, as removable batteries became less common, SIM trays were moved to the outside of phones. Early models using this setup would often show a network error if you swapped SIMs while the phone was on, but they quickly became hot-swappable and this was no longer a problem.
You don't even need to switch your device off completely to make the phone refresh its carrier settings from the card. You'll get a similar result if you turn on airplane mode, wait 30 seconds before swapping the SIM and turn airplane mode off again once the new SIM is inserted. This should prevent any carrier hiccups during the process.
A warning on SD cards
Unlike the iPhone, some Android devices still include a microSD card slot. In some cases, this is in the same tray as the SIM, though placement varies. If this is the case for you, as when ejecting an external drive, it's important to unmount the microSD card before removing the SIM to prevent losing data. On Samsung devices: open the My Files app, find the SD Card, tap the three-dot menu next to it and choose Unmount. Search the Settings app or check online documentation if you're not sure how this works for your device.
So while the benefits are slight, switching off your phone when replacing the SIM can prevent software-related glitches. If you don't want to power down, use airplane mode instead. And in case you encounter a network error after swapping, always try restarting your device first.

title_en: What to check if your Nintendo Switch 2 isn't connecting to the TV
title_fa: What to check if your Nintendo Switch 2 isn't connecting to the TV
excerpt_en: Your Nintendo Switch 2 is made to project its display to a TV. If it's not working, there are some things you should check.
excerpt_fa: Your Nintendo Switch 2 is made to project its display to a TV. If it's not working, there are some things you should check.
content_en:
What to check if your Nintendo Switch 2 isn't connecting to the TV
Getting a black screen? Try these steps.
One of the best things about the Nintendo Switch is the ability to play on its built-in screen for on-the-go gaming and then plug into a bigger screen at home for a more cinematic experience.
But getting the Switch 2 to play nice with a TV isn't always foolproof, and there are some compatibility-related snags you can run into. If you encounter a black TV screen or an unresponsive console, there are a few key things you can try yourself before pinging Nintendo support.
Make sure your power source works
Nintendo recommends powering off your TV and disconnecting all cables from the Switch 2 dock to start the troubleshooting process. That means fully disconnecting the AC adapter from the dock and the wall outlet, removing the handheld from the dock and keeping everything unplugged for about 30 seconds.
The Switch 2 dock has three ports on the back behind its removable panel. The top port is for AC power. After you've unplugged everything, you can plug the AC adapter back into the dock and then into the wall socket. Make sure the handheld screen faces the front of the dock and is slotted in fully.
It might seem obvious, but it's important to check that your dock is fully plugged in and receiving power via its AC adapter to establish a TV connection. Split cables can cause power issues, so check for any fraying or visible damage.
If the cables look good, ensure that the USB plug side of the AC adapter is fully seated in the port and plug the other end of the power supply into the wall. A dead wall outlet won't be able to charge your handheld or connect to an external display.
But if you suspect your wall outlet could be the issue, check to see if your outlet is delivering power by attempting to charge another device using a different charger in that same socket.
If your Switch 2 isn't using the Nintendo AC adapter that came with the device, ensure any third-party AC adapter meets the console's power needs. The Switch 2 requires more power than the original Nintendo Switch. It needs an adapter delivering a minimum of 54W to support a continuous TV connection. Nintendo sells Switch 2 accessories, including compatible AC adapters for $35 each on its official website, in case any of your components are missing or broken.
Test the HDMI connection
Check your AC adapter's compatibility and ensure it can charge your handheld, and then move on to troubleshooting the HDMI connection with your TV.
Plug one end of an Ultra High Speed (UHS) dual-end HDMI cable into the HDMI-out port on your Nintendo Switch 2's dock. The Switch 2 comes with a UHS HDMI cable, which supports 48Gbps bandwidth and HDMI 2.1 connections. Third-party cables can also work if they support UHS. You won't be able to use a lower-speed HDMI cable or the cable that came with a first-generation Nintendo Switch, unfortunately.
Plug the other end of your UHS HDMI cable into an HDMI-in port on your TV. It's best to use an HDMI 2.1 port, as it enables up to 8K resolution at a 60Hz refresh rate (or 4K at 120Hz) compared to the HDMI 1.0 ports. While UHS HDMI cables are technically backward-compatible with HDMI 1.0 ports, the port will limit the output quality, and 4K resolution and high refresh rates won't be possible. However, you'd have to have a pretty old device for it to have HDMI 1.0. The 2.0 specification (which supports 4K) was released in 2013.
Your TV model may not have its HDMI port type marked, however, so you will have to verify with your manufacturer if your TV has HDMI 2.1 ports. Most LG OLED TVs, for example, have multiple HDMI 2.1 ports that are more than sufficient to support the Switch 2, which can transmit either a 4K video output at a 60Hz refresh rate or 1080p at a 120Hz refresh rate.
Check your TV's HDMI settings
It's also worth digging into your TV's HDMI settings if your Switch still isn't connecting. Turn on your TV with your regular remote and look under picture settings, advanced settings or output settings menus to see if your TV offers an Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), a gaming mode, HDMI Ultra HD Deep Color or Input Signal Plus to enable for the port the Switch 2 is plugged into.
Then, select the HDMI input that matches the port where you inserted the cable. If the Switch 2 doesn't show onscreen automatically, try pressing the handheld screen's power button while it remains slotted in the dock. And make sure your controllers are charged so they can connect to your device.
If you're still having trouble, Nintendo suggests testing another UHS HDMI cable, other HDMI ports on your TV or another TV, if possible, to help determine what's causing your connection issue.
Check the handheld and its settings
If your Switch 2 still isn't connecting to your TV, it could be due to an issue with the handheld, its software or settings. Remove the handheld from the dock and try turning it on. Make sure the latest software update is installed and update the device if needed by navigating to System Settings > System > System Update.
You can also try modifying your settings via the Switch 2 handheld's menu. Try changing System Settings > Display > TV Resolution to Automatic or the resolution that matches your TV's output. Also toggle on System Settings > Display > Match TV Power State, as this can automatically turn the TV screen on when the console is powered on and docked. It's worth noting, however, that older TVs may not be able to wake using this feature.
Contact support
If you've tried all of the above and are still having issues getting your Switch 2 to work with your TV, contact Nintendo support for help. You might have to mail in your dock and console so Nintendo can look into the problem for you.

Then, select the HDMI input that matches the port where you inserted the cable. If the Switch 2 doesn't show onscreen automatically, try pressing the handheld screen's power button while it remains slotted in the dock. And make sure your controllers are charged so they can connect to your device.
If you're still having trouble, Nintendo suggests testing another UHS HDMI cable, other HDMI ports on your TV or another TV, if possible, to help determine what's causing your connection issue.
Check the handheld and its settings
If your Switch 2 still isn't connecting to your TV, it could be due to an issue with the handheld, its software or settings. Remove the handheld from the dock and try turning it on. Make sure the latest software update is installed and update the device if needed by navigating to System Settings > System > System Update.
You can also try modifying your settings via the Switch 2 handheld's menu. Try changing System Settings > Display > TV Resolution to Automatic or the resolution that matches your TV's output. Also toggle on System Settings > Display > Match TV Power State, as this can automatically turn the TV screen on when the console is powered on and docked. It's worth noting, however, that older TVs may not be able to wake using this feature.
Contact support
If you've tried all of the above and are still having issues getting your Switch 2 to work with your TV, contact Nintendo support for help. You might have to mail in your dock and console so Nintendo can look into the problem for you.

title_en: OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, but the body isn't the real challenge
title_fa: OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, but the body isn't the real challenge
excerpt_en: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wants a humanoid that can operate in a world designed for people, though the CEO says a robot 'brain' is a much bigger challenge.
excerpt_fa: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wants a humanoid that can operate in a world designed for people, though the CEO says a robot 'brain' is a much bigger challenge.
content_en:
OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, but the body isn't the real challenge
Figuring out how the 'brain' will work will take a lot of time.
While OpenAI is already busy with the development of AI models and new consumer hardware, CEO Sam Altman and his team apparently have time for one more project: a humanoid robot.
On the Sources podcast, Altman explained that the human form is logical because "the world is very much designed for people." Doors, keyboards and tools are all designed around a certain type of body, and a robot that can move around in the same spaces should probably have a similar form factor. As Altman put it, "matching that form factor seems good."
When asked if OpenAI will actually build one, his response was much more succinct: "We will." However, Altman isn't so concerned with the nitty-gritty details of what that robot looks like. Those questions are "less important than really figuring out ... the brain that makes the robot work," he said. Basically, giving a machine two arms and two legs doesn't get you very far if it doesn't know what to do with them.
This is still some distance from becoming a product. Altman told Fortune: "I think we'll have a cool demo in 2027 ... I don't think there will be robots walking the streets for a few years longer." OpenAI hasn't disclosed what that demo will showcase, what its humanoid will look like or when anyone outside the company will get close to one.
The 'brain' has to make the hardware useful
Calling it a robot "brain" almost makes the problem sound neat, but it isn't.
A capable humanoid must be able to understand what its cameras and sensors are seeing, interpret an instruction, decide how to carry it out, coordinate its body and then correct itself when the real world introduces something inconvenient. When picking up a mug, for instance, it needs to identify the mug, find the handle, estimate the grip and exert the correct amount of force to lift it. Otherwise, you're left with a coffee spill and a floor-cleaning job.
OpenAI is already recruiting people to address those issues. Its robotics roles span motion control, state estimation, actuator control and whole-robot behavior, as well as the machine-learning infrastructure to train physical AI systems.
There's a bit of history here as well. OpenAI's Dactyl research project taught a robotic hand how to manipulate real objects, with its training done entirely in simulation. The company later applied the technique to a Rubik's Cube, an early example of the same headache that plagues robotics companies to this day: a model can learn what should happen through its software, but physics has the final say.
OpenAI still has to build the body
Altman's focus on intelligence shouldn't be mistaken for OpenAI treating the hardware as an afterthought. The company's robotics job listings indicate it is working on custom electromechanical actuators that include motors, transmissions, sensing and thermal systems, while other positions cover manufacturing and the supply chain needed to eventually produce hardware at scale. That's quite a bit of work for the "less important" half of the robot.
OpenAI is also not entering uncharted territory. Tesla has been working on Optimus for years, and XPENG recently had its IRON humanoid autonomously walk off the production line after being assembled. Both are good reminders that even smart software has to coax a very complex set of motors and joints into action.
OpenAI's own plans seem to begin at a more down-to-earth level than placing a robotic roommate in every home. One of its robotics job postings states that the company's short-term objective is to create general-purpose robots that can help skilled workers build infrastructure, and its long-term goal is to develop a personal robot that can help with a much wider variety of tasks.
If you're already imagining a physical form of ChatGPT with knees doing the dishes, you may not need to remove your dishwasher just yet. OpenAI hasn't announced an actual robot yet, or a consumer price, subscription model, release date or robot-specific privacy framework. Those questions get a bit more real-world if a future OpenAI machine is equipped with cameras and microphones and allowed to roam around someone's house.
That said, OpenAI's careers page currently lists 27 robotics openings.

title_en: These Samsung Galaxy tablets are in their last year of software support
title_fa: These Samsung Galaxy tablets are in their last year of software support
excerpt_en: Samsung's latest software update commitment for its tablets is great, but older devices can't take advantage of it.
excerpt_fa: Samsung's latest software update commitment for its tablets is great, but older devices can't take advantage of it.
content_en:
These Samsung Galaxy tablets are in their last year of software support
These tablets are the last ones released before Samsung's more generous support policy.
Back in the TouchWiz era, Samsung's reputation for timely software updates wasn't exactly the best. It's thus great to see how far the brand has come in delivering faster updates and providing longer software support for its devices. Samsung is now one of the few Android manufacturers that offers a generously long software support policy, with its recent Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra benefiting from seven years of OS and security updates. Not every tablet Samsung has sold in previous years enjoys that kind of longevity, though.
2026 marks the final release of major Android updates for the Galaxy Tab S9, S9+, S9 Ultra, S9 FE and S9 FE+. These tablets will receive the One UI 9 update, which is based on Android 17. The Galaxy Tab S9 series arrived in 2023 running One UI 5.1 (Android 13), with Samsung promising four generations of major OS updates and five years of security patches for these devices. They should continue to receive security updates until sometime in 2028.
The Galaxy Tab S8, S8+ and S8 Ultra (released in February 2022) have already received their final major OS upgrade with One UI 8, which is based on Android 16. Security updates should continue until February 2027. Android 16 is also the last major update for the Galaxy Tab A9 and A9+, which were released in October 2023. Despite being a bit newer, the Galaxy Tab A9 series has already received its final major OS update, likely because it was a budget-oriented offering. It will still receive another year of security updates.
What about newer Samsung tablets?
Fortunately, newer Galaxy Tab models come with longer software support cycles. Samsung began its seven-year software update policy with the Galaxy Tab S10 series that launched in 2024. The newer Galaxy Tab S11 and S12 models offer the same commitment. Surprisingly, even Samsung's budget Galaxy Tab A11 and A11+ devices, which released in 2025, are eligible for seven years of Android and security updates. If you're buying from Samsung's current catalog of tablets, you don't have to worry about having software updates dropped anytime soon.
Samsung also sells rugged tablets under its Galaxy Tab Active lineup, which are marketed primarily towards business and enterprise customers. These devices have different software update policies. The Galaxy Tab Active5 was launched in 2024 with a four-year commitment to Android OS updates and five years of security updates. Since it shipped with Android 14, it should be good for updates through Android 18, with security patches continuing until 2029.
Be aware that not every device from Samsung receives OS updates at the same time. Rollout schedules vary depending on your tablet's model and region. So if you aren't seeing the One UI 9 update on your Galaxy Tab yet, it doesn't mean you've been left out. Check for Android or security updates on your Samsung tablet by navigating to Settings > Software update > Download and install. If there's a pending update available, tap Install now.

title_en: Why your Wi-Fi speeds can drop in the evening, and what to do about it
title_fa: Why your Wi-Fi speeds can drop in the evening, and what to do about it
excerpt_en: Everyone getting online at the same time can slam the network, but working around these slowdowns is possible with a few tricks.
excerpt_fa: Everyone getting online at the same time can slam the network, but working around these slowdowns is possible with a few tricks.
content_en:
Why your Wi-Fi speeds can drop in the evening, and what to do about it
The internet gets slower when everyone is trying to use it, but you have some workarounds.
One of the most frustrating parts of troubleshooting slow Wi-Fi is that almost by nature, network conditions are rarely consistent. Say you're trying to diagnose issues with poor video quality on Netflix. Router issues could be to blame, but there might also be trouble with your internet service or the infrastructure on Netflix's end. You might also discover that your spouse is torrenting files en masse, leaving little bandwidth for a 4K HDR stream.
Some consistency, albeit unwanted, can come in the form of evening slowdowns. It's a terrible "coincidence:" you just got off work and all you want is to kick back with a movie or game, but your speeds are way slower than usual. Or maybe you work from home in the evenings and suffer from low-quality video calls.
As it turns out, the explanation for these slowdowns is relatively straightforward. Solving them can be harder, possibly dependent on power-cycling equipment or reconfiguring your apps and setup. But ultimately, you may be dependent on the whims of your neighbors.
The causes of evening slowdowns, and how to fix them
The source of the problem is most likely a traffic jam. Unless you live in a rural area or an especially sparse suburb, there are other like-minded people nearby, probably coming back from work (or school) at roughly the same time and getting online. With cable internet, this increases overall congestion because many houses in the same neighborhood share bandwidth. It's not as much of a problem with fiber internet, which offers far greater bandwidth.
Tons of people getting online simultaneously also increases competition for the frequency bands Wi-Fi routers share in common. In a large apartment complex, there may be dozens or hundreds of devices fighting to compete on the same frequencies.
One potential fix is power-cycling your modem and router. Unplug them for at least 30 seconds, then plug them back in again, waiting for the modem to reconnect before restarting your router (assuming it's a separate piece of equipment). Doing this forces the devices to clear their caches and acquire fresh, potentially more optimal connections. The results aren't guaranteed to be faster, but they can be, and it's unlikely that performance will get any worse.
If you haven't already, you might also consider changing router settings to create separate SSIDs (network names) for each of your router's bands, then forcing your most data-hungry devices over to 5GHz or 6GHz if they support it. That's because the 2.4GHz band is not only popular, but long-range, and easily congestible due to the way its channels work. It's even vulnerable to interference from other electronics like appliances and Bluetooth devices. It's best to reserve 2.4GHz for smart home accessories, which need range more than raw speed, and can afford to blip out for a second or two.
Changing your network usage habits may be inevitable
Realistically, you may sometimes have adapt your lifestyle to network conditions, rather than the other way around. This might be limited to using your own internet bandwidth more wisely when everyone is at home using it, or it could require you working around what your neighborhood is doing.
Have software updates run overnight, rather than downloading them immediately. Configuring updates to be automatic can do the trick, as many platforms rely on your usage habits to pick the ideal window. If this isn't reliable, either schedule them or make it a habit to manually checking for updates before you go to bed. The same goes for file downloads in general — it can be almost cruel to your neighbors to start torrenting during waking hours. Don't run huge cloud sync operations when everyone else in your family is online.
Postponing some activities by an hour or two may be enough. Think about what the people around you are probably doing. When a popular show has a new episode, trying to stream it the instant it goes live can be an exercise in futility. Likewise, if you're trying to play an online game like PUBG or Galactic Racer, consider waiting until most school-aged kids are off to bed.
Lastly, consider switching some devices over to wired Ethernet if they support it and don't need mobility. While going wired won't solve issues with general internet traffic, Ethernet is effectively invulnerable to range or band congestion woes, which means more stable connections for gaming and faster download speeds on computers. The biggest concern is running cables to reach your router.
