title_en: How to keep your smart home running even if the internet goes down
title_fa: How to keep your smart home running even if the internet goes down
excerpt_en: Smart home products most often harness Wi-Fi to function. But what can you do if you lose internet frequently?
excerpt_fa: Smart home products most often harness Wi-Fi to function. But what can you do if you lose internet frequently?
content_en:
How to keep your smart home running even if the internet goes down
Your smart devices don't have to stop working when your Wi-Fi does.
With Apple finally developing new smart home products, now's a great time to remind everyone that though the technology can improve your home's look and convenience, there are also a few hazards involved. If you're overly ambitious with your routines, for example, smart bulbs might switch off when people need them. Once, while we installed a smart thermostat, the heat ran dangerously out of control until we fixed an obscure flaw.
For many of you, the biggest issue is going to be offline resilience. When internet access goes down, some smart home accessories can go "dumb," either maintaining their last state or failing to work at all. Usually, this is just an inconvenience. If you're counting on an accessory for health or security, however, this can become a legitimate crisis.
Thankfully, there are ways of building a smart home around offline automation without investing in the custom systems you find in mansions. It's just a matter of anchoring your gear around the right peripherals and protocols. And if you caught the pun just now, you're one step ahead.
Let the hubs do the talking
The reason so many accessories turn dumb is that they connect directly to Wi-Fi to fetch instructions from a cloud server. Wi-Fi accessories are often the easiest to set up — if the internet goes down, however, or if your Wi-Fi router encounters hiccups, they may have no way of storing and triggering automations on their own. They may not even switch on or off at scheduled times, which you'd think would be dead simple.
Whenever possible, then, it's best to turn to accessories that route everything through a local hub. These hubs still connect to the internet, but they can store and process many automations locally as long as everything still has power. The only major exceptions are automations that depend on live data, like current weather conditions, or involve sharing data remotely. If you're going to install a smart security system and internet outages are a regular issue, cellular backup is a must.
These hubs can take many forms. If you're using Apple Home, for example, HomePods and Apple TVs can act as home hubs, enabling both remote access and local automations. Some security cameras can record to local hub storage, even if they have to go online to trigger alerts or perform advanced functions. Matter-enabled smart speakers and displays are capable of executing offline commands, though in practice, companies like Amazon and Google don't really exploit this. We discovered this the hard way.
The most bulletproof hubs tend to be those that link local hardware not through Wi-Fi, but through Thread, Zigbee or Z-Wave radios. All three are low-power, low-bandwidth mesh standards. A hub can often connect many compatible accessories simultaneously, and the mesh aspect means that accessories farther away from the hub won't drop off. Thread is preferable, since some Wi-Fi accessories can act as Thread "border routers," but we've had great experiences with Zigbee-based hubs like the Philips Hue Bridge. The only real problem with these technologies is that their low bandwidth limits them to things like lights, locks and sensors.
What about the power problem?
The ideal setup would involve using an entirely hub-based smart home ecosystem paired with whole-home power backup. That's not realistic for most people, unfortunately. Some accessories don't exist in a hub-compatible form, and more importantly, whole-home battery systems cost thousands or tens of thousands of dollars. Assuming that's in your budget, it might still not be worth the outlay unless your job or safety is at stake. You can deal with your soundbar or light panels being down for 30 minutes.
A workable compromise involves hunting for accessories with their own redundancy, whether that means batteries, backup controls or both. The Philips Hue Go, for example, can connect to a Hue Bridge, but includes a battery to operate as a portable lamp as well. It can keep shining for hours when it loses AC power, and it cycles through some basic effects using an onboard button or app-based Bluetooth commands. Smart thermostats will always keep operating on their last schedule as long as your HVAC system is powered.
You won't be able to secure redundancy for every smart home accessory. But if you think ahead when shopping, at least some of them should keep running 24/7. Don't just pick the cheapest or slickest options at hand.

The Philips Hue Go, for example, can connect to a Hue Bridge, but includes a battery to operate as a portable lamp as well. It can keep shining for hours when it loses AC power, and it cycles through some basic effects using an onboard button or app-based Bluetooth commands. Smart thermostats will always keep operating on their last schedule as long as your HVAC system is powered.
You won't be able to secure redundancy for every smart home accessory. But if you think ahead when shopping, at least some of them should keep running 24/7. Don't just pick the cheapest or slickest options at hand.

title_en: Why it's important to monitor your PC's background processes
title_fa: Why it's important to monitor your PC's background processes
excerpt_en: What your PC is doing in the background doesn't need to be a mystery. Learn about what's happening and how to spot when something looks wrong.
excerpt_fa: What your PC is doing in the background doesn't need to be a mystery. Learn about what's happening and how to spot when something looks wrong.
content_en:
Why it's important to monitor your PC's background processes
Knowing what normally runs on your PC helps you spot when something isn't right.
Your PC is always doing something, even when you've closed all the app windows from your desktop. Windows is checking for updates and keeping everything moving under the hood, with other apps still running quietly in the background. Ideally, this is all happening with a useful purpose. But some apps or services are always going to use more processing power or memory than you expect, taking up resources that could otherwise be available to apps you actually want to use.
With that in mind, it's smart to get into the habit of checking your PC's background processes. When you know what's supposed to run, it'll help you spot the unusual. This doesn't mean you need to watch the numbers all day, and a long running list isn't bad by itself. Instead, monitoring them means you can spot processes causing problems or sucking up resources on your PC. That'll help you decide what to leave alone and what to close, especially when your PC starts to feel slow.
Use Task Manager to keep an eye on your PC
Background processes are programs, or parts of programs, running without you directly interacting with them. They're handling everything: mundane jobs like syncing files and installing updates, as well as important visual elements like the windows you're clicking.
There's one place you should look first when you want to see what's running on your PC: Task Manager. Alongside your open apps, you'll find all running background processes, including system-level Windows tasks. It shows how much CPU power and memory is in use for each, along with disk activity and network bandwidth.
There are a couple of ways to open it. Ctrl + Shift + Esc on your keyboard is a quick shortcut, although pressing Ctrl + Alt + Delete > Task Manager will get you there too. You can also right-click the Start button or an empty area of the taskbar and select Task Manager.
Begin on the Processes tab (accessible through the left sidebar). Clicking the Name header to sort by app title is handy, as this groups running processes by type (active Apps, then Background processes and finally Windows processes). Click any of the column headings to sort using them instead, bringing the heaviest users to the top.
Understand what your background processes are doing
You'll recognize some of the entries right away. Expect to see apps like Chrome listed, plus Task Manager itself. Others are less obvious: a game launcher, for instance, might leave an updater running after you've closed its main window. You'll also find services that Windows relies on, so don't assume something is unnecessary just because you don't recognize it.
Chrome is a good example, as it has plenty of background processes that run while you're using it. Each tab has a process, along with others that handle features like hardware acceleration and extensions. Chrome's own Task Manager tool (Shift + Esc) gives a clearer idea of what each process is responsible for.
Don't expect a one-size-fits-all number of background processes; this depends on your PC's specs. Obviously, a PC with slower hardware is more likely to be negatively hit by busy processes. You can watch this in real-time by keeping an eye on Task Manager. When it reports sustained activity, you're able to watch and potentially stop anything that's hogging resources.
It's a good idea to check when your PC is running normally, too, as that gives you a point of comparison to know when an app is using more resources than normal.
Close unnecessary apps to free up resources
If you've spotted a process or two that's sucking up your RAM or maxing out your CPU, you may be thinking it's time to hit the kill switch. While you can use Task Manager to kill running processes, avoid doing this as your first choice, as there might be a reason why an app is suddenly using resources. Consider a game launcher that's not showing on your screen, but your disk activity is up, as is your CPU and RAM usage. While that seems bad in isolation, it's explained by the platform downloading and installing updates in the background.
When you can, always exit an app cleanly using the X in the top-right corner, or its own option under File > Quit or similar. Check the system tray at the bottom-right of the screen for icons representing background apps to close them properly, too.
When an app won't close normally, then Task Manager comes into play: right-click its entry in Task Manager's Processes list and click End task. Ending a task here is forcible, meaning an app won't have a chance to make sure you've saved your work and end gracefully. But when an app has crashed, that's probably unavoidable anyway.
Use Google to identify any services you don't immediately recognize; with names like svchost.exe for various background Windows services, it's not worth guessing what they do. Right-click any process and select Open File Location to see where it's stored.
Performance isn't the only reason to check what you've got running. If you're concerned about something running on your PC, especially if it's stubborn enough that killing it in Task Manager doesn't work, give your PC a quick health check for any viruses or malware. Windows has built-in protection with Microsoft Defender, which you can access via Windows Security > Virus & threat protection. You'll want to select Scan options > Microsoft Defender Antivirus (offline scan) > Scan now.
The offline scan requires a PC restart. The scan runs in its own, separate environment, where any stubborn malware won't be able to stop itself from being quarantined or deleted.
Cut back on background activity while you're gaming
Gamers have a particular interest in reducing the amount of background activity on their PCs. Every system resource that isn't used by other apps can be used to improve in-game performance. Downloads are a good place to start — don't run multiple launchers...

title_en: Don't throw away your old PlayStation — Do this instead
title_fa: Don't throw away your old PlayStation — Do this instead
excerpt_en: Older PlayStations may be past their prime, but there are several ways you can make use of these consoles.
excerpt_fa: Older PlayStations may be past their prime, but there are several ways you can make use of these consoles.
content_en:
Don't throw away your old PlayStation — Do this instead
It doesn't need to end up in a landfill.
It can be sad to watch the PlayStation you spent hours fighting the hardest bosses with eventually fall out of use. But the fact that you no longer use your old PlayStation as much doesn't make it useless. So, don't throw away your old PlayStation; you can find other ways to give it purpose.
Thankfully, finding practical ways to repurpose your old PlayStation console can be pretty easy. With the right steps and a few hours, you can turn your beloved old PlayStation into a media center for watching your favorite shows or reuse its parts, among several other things. And if you feel there's no use to be had, you can sell it for cash or recycle it rather than throwing it away. Even old consoles like the PS2 can still be sold for cash today, so anything's better than your old PlayStation contributing to the already bad e-waste problem.
Turn your old PlayStation into a media center
Your PlayStation can access media in three main ways. First, there are streaming services. You can load up your old PlayStation with your favorite streaming apps and services. How you download them varies depending on your exact PlayStation. If your console is a PlayStation 3, this route is mostly closed, as many major streaming services have already stopped supporting the PS3.
If streaming services don't tickle your fancy, you can turn to physical media. Old PlayStations even as far back as the PS2 can play DVDs with the same disc drives used for games. The PS2 tops out at DVDs, while the PS3 and PS4 can handle both DVDs and Blu-rays. So, if you still use discs, your old PlayStation can find new life as a dedicated movie player.
Beyond discs and streaming apps, you can simply play media from USB drives. Before you plug the drive in, you'll need to format the drive to exFAT (or FAT32 specifically for the PS3) if it's in NTFS, then move the media files into folders on the drive. On the PS4, you'll need to install the Media Player app first. Next, plug it into your old PlayStation and enjoy.
Reuse its parts
Your old PlayStation might not be useful to you anymore in its entirety, but there are certain parts that you can easily reuse. Namely, the controllers, cables and even the hard drive.
PlayStation controllers, especially the DualShock 4, are compatible with a wide range of devices, from phones to tablets to PCs and even some new-gen consoles. You can even connect the DualShock 4 to an Amazon Fire TV Stick and use it for cloud gaming or even as a makeshift remote. Your old PS4 controller can easily become a gaming controller that works across your devices. The PS3's controller (DualShock 3) has similar functionality, but it works with fewer devices and the connection process isn't as easy as the DualShock 4”s.
If you're willing to dig a little deeper and remove a few screws along the way, you can harvest your PlayStation's hard drive and convert it into external storage for your other devices and files. Sony designed the PlayStation's hard drive to be user-replaceable, so you won't need expert-level technical skills to get it out. Once it's out, all you need is a quick reformatting and a USB enclosure for the drive, and you're good to go. Since you're putting the console out of commission anyway, you might as well repurpose the HDMI and power cables, too. Once you've pulled the parts you want, recycle what's left of the console responsibly.
Sell your old PlayStation
Yes, even your old PlayStation console can still be worth money if you know where to sell it. Selling your old PlayStation is a great way to get cash while getting rid of a console you no longer use, and, for most people, there are three main ways to go about this.
First and probably the most popular is trading in your PlayStation to retailers like Best Buy, Amazon and GameStop. This is the most convenient way to sell your PlayStation, but that convenience comes at a cost. For one, you'll get lowball offers, and most big-box retailers only pay out with store credit, which isn't that helpful if you don't plan on shopping there.
The second option is buyback sites like Back Market Trade-in. As the name implies, these companies buy used tech, including PlayStation consoles, for cash, with no listing or haggling involved. The upside is they're convenient, pay actual cash and typically value old PlayStations more than big-box retailers. But there are shipping risks, and you'll have to wait longer to get paid compared to retailer trade-in.
The third option is selling your PlayStation on marketplaces like Swappa and eBay. With this method, you stand to gain more from your old PlayStation compared with buybacks and big-box retailers. But handling a marketplace sale is typically inconvenient, takes longer and is more tasking than you'd encounter selling to a buyback or a big-box retailer.
So, sell on a marketplace if you want the most cash for your old PlayStation, sell to a big-box retailer if you want the most convenient option and sell to a buyback if you want a middle ground. Buyback will get you a better offer than big-box retailers while still being more convenient than selling on a marketplace.
Hand it down, donate or recycle your old PlayStation
If your PlayStation console no longer has a place in your setup and you feel it's not worth selling, then it might be time for ownership to change hands. Instead of throwing it away, you can hand it down to a younger person who'd give your old PlayStation the love and care it deserves.
If you don't have anyone to hand it down to, then donating it is your next best option. There are a number of charity organizations that can put your old PlayStation to good use and get it to people who'd appreciate it. Gamers Outreach, for example, collects certain donated consoles and gives them to children at hospitals. Before you send off your PlayStation as a donation to any organization, make sure to do your due diligence; check...

title_en: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns
title_fa: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns
excerpt_en: A Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web.
excerpt_fa: A Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web.
content_en:
Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.
According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab, this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)
However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.
“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”

title_en: The Tesla Roadster is far from the first car to use fans for downforce
title_fa: The Tesla Roadster is far from the first car to use fans for downforce
excerpt_en: Here are some of the other, older vehicles that use fans for downforce like the Tesla Roadster does.
excerpt_fa: Here are some of the other, older vehicles that use fans for downforce like the Tesla Roadster does.
content_en:
The Tesla Roadster is far from the first car to use fans for downforce
We list some of those cars, including the historic Chaparral 2J.
Tesla demonstrated the long-awaited next-gen Roadster with some wild stunts, starting with making the car drive up a C-shaped ramp and stop in the middle of the part perpendicular to the ground. It drove slow enough and stopped long enough to make it look like it was hanging upside down. After that, the Roadster jumped off the ramp, flipped itself upright, floated a bit and landed safely on the ground.
On its website, Tesla explained that the Roadster defied gravity by using a multi-mode fan and ground sealing system that acts as a "downforce generator." It pulls air from underneath the vehicle and provides the suction needed to hold the car upside down, at any speed. The automaker says those powered fans, along with the vehicle's retractable rear wing, provide the necessary downforce, or the force that pushes a vehicle into the ground.
The new Roadster, however, isn't the first car that uses a fan system to generate downforce. When Tesla unveiled the Roadster, McMurtry Automotive responded with a cheeky "Welcome to the club" on Instagram, with a video of its Spéirling hanging upside down from a platform. McMurtry's suction technology called Downforce-on-Demand has two fans that suck air out from under the car. And even before Spéirling, other vehicles have employed fans for downforce.
Chaparral 2J and Brabham BT46
Way back in 1970, American racing drivers Jim Hall and Hap Sharp entered the Can-Am Championship series with a car that looked like a box with wheels. It was called the Chaparral 2J, a prototype powered by modified 7.6-liter Chevrolet V8 engine. According to Revs Institute Automedia, the vehicle's suction technology started as the "Suspension Test Vehicle" project at Chevrolet, until Hall asked its developer Don Gates to join his team.
The Chaparral 2J's suction system had two fans adapted from a military tank engine. It had a "skirt" made from transparent polycarbonate sheets that created an enclosed area underneath the car. That allowed the fans to generate 1.25 g to 1.5 g of suction as the fans pulled in air from that enclosed space. To note, Tesla says the Roadster is capable of generating up to 2 gs of downforce.
Then there was the Brabham BT46, also known as the "Fan Car," which was an F1 racing car designed by South African-British racer Gordon Murray for the 1978 season. It designers installed a fan on the vehicle and claimed it was mainly for cooling to satisfy F1 regulations, but they took inspiration from the Chaparral 2J and Tyrrell 008, another F1 car with a fan that ultimately didn't work out.
Specifically, the BT46 had a series of clutches that connected to a large single fan at the rear. It had skirts, just like the Chaparral 2J, that covered the gaps between the bottom of the car and the ground. This allowed the fan to extract air from beneath the car, creating a suction. In BT46's case, the faster the vehicle, the stronger the suction effect. The Brabham BT46 only raced once at the 1978 Swedish Grand Prix and won the event.
McMurtry Spéirling
McMurtry's Spéirling is an electric sports car that the automaker unveiled in 2025. The company demonstrated it at McMurtry headquarters in England, where the vehicle was shown to be able to cling upside down to a rotating platform completely unsupported.
McMurtry Automotive unveiled the final production version of the Spéirling Pure in July 2026. Like the Roadster, Spéirling's technology can generate enough downforce that allows it to cling to a surface at any speed, even at a standstill. This gives the vehicle the power to corner at more than 3g, according to the company.
The company will produce only 100 of the vehicles, with prices starting at $132,300, and the first customer deliveries are expected to go out out before the end of this year. Meanwhile, Elon Musk said the Roadster is going into production in 2028, with reservations now open. The base Roadster will cost you $50,000 to reserve, while the "Thrust" trim level with the the suction system and acceleration thrusters costs $250,000 to reserve.

Specifically, the BT46 had a series of clutches that connected to a large single fan at the rear. It had skirts, just like the Chaparral 2J, that covered the gaps between the bottom of the car and the ground. This allowed the fan to extract air from beneath the car, creating a suction. In BT46's case, the faster the vehicle, the stronger the suction effect. The Brabham BT46 only raced once at the 1978 Swedish Grand Prix and won the event.
McMurtry Spéirling
McMurtry's Spéirling is an electric sports car that the automaker unveiled in 2025. The company demonstrated it at McMurtry headquarters in England, where the vehicle was shown to be able to cling upside down to a rotating platform completely unsupported.
McMurtry Automotive unveiled the final production version of the Spéirling Pure in July 2026. Like the Roadster, Spéirling's technology can generate enough downforce that allows it to cling to a surface at any speed, even at a standstill. This gives the vehicle the power to corner at more than 3g, according to the company.
The company will produce only 100 of the vehicles, with prices starting at $132,300, and the first customer deliveries are expected to go out out before the end of this year. Meanwhile, Elon Musk said the Roadster is going into production in 2028, with reservations now open. The base Roadster will cost you $50,000 to reserve, while the "Thrust" trim level with the the suction system and acceleration thrusters costs $250,000 to reserve.

title_en: TikTok permanently bans ‘Musk’ documentary advertising account
title_fa: TikTok permanently bans ‘Musk’ documentary advertising account
excerpt_en: A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms.
excerpt_fa: A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms.
content_en:
A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms, with TikTok banning the film’s advertising account.
According to a story in The Hollywood Reporter, the documentary’s distributor Bleecker Street was recently notified by TikTok that the account had received a “permanent suspension” due to its political content. TechCrunch has reached out to TikTok for comment.
Ads promoting the trailer for “Musk” — directed by Oscar-winner filmmaker Alex Gibney — were initially rejected by Meta and YouTube as well, though those platforms eventually allowed the ad, with Meta blaming the rejection on “an error.” Gibney recently confirmed that the film’s international distributor Universal had wavered in its plans to release “Musk,” though it’s now moving forward.
X, which Musk owns, has refused to carry ads for “Musk.” TikTok’s U.S. operations are partly owned by Larry Ellison — who, like Musk, has been a notable supporter of President Donald Trump.
“Musk” opened in just four theaters last weekend and is now rolling out more broadly. Next year, it’s supposed to stream on HBO — now part of Paramount/Skydance and led by Ellison’s son David.

title_en: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
title_fa: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
excerpt_en: The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year.
excerpt_fa: The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year.
content_en:
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.
Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.
Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.
Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”
One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”
In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.
Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.
The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

excerpt_en: Just ahead of the wider release of Alex Gibney's Musk documentary, TikTok has banned the film's social media account from its platform. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the film's distributor, Bleecker Street, was...

content_en:
Just ahead of the wider release of Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, TikTok has banned the film’s social media account from its platform. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, was informed Friday afternoon that a “permanent suspension” was imminent. Bleecker Street has not yet responded to a request for comment from The Verge.
TikTok bans Musk documentary account
Larry Ellison’s TikTok has shut down the promotional account for Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary.
Larry Ellison’s TikTok has shut down the promotional account for Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary.
While TikTok has no official affiliation with Elon Musk, part owner Larry Ellison appears in the film via a text message offering to help Musk fund his Twitter purchase.
Last month, YouTube, Meta, X, and TikTok all faced backlash for rejecting ads for the film. YouTube and Google quickly reversed course, calling it an “error.” However, TikTok and X have refused to change their stance, and neither platform has allowed paid advertisements for the film.
Banning the documentary’s account, however, marks a serious escalation, and one laced with a dash of irony — shortly before the account was removed, it posted that people should see the movie “before it gets shut down.”

title_en: Leaked gameplay purports to show a canceled Assassin's Creed game set in ancient China
title_fa: Leaked gameplay purports to show a canceled Assassin's Creed game set in ancient China
excerpt_en: At least there's still Assassin's Creed Jade to look forward to.
excerpt_fa: At least there's still Assassin's Creed Jade to look forward to.
content_en:
Leaked gameplay purports to show a canceled Assassin's Creed game set in ancient China
At least there’s still Assassin’s Creed Jade to look forward to.
A mainline entry in the Assassin's Creed franchise set in ancient China might sound too good to be true. According to the some leaked footage of a reportedly canceled title called Assassin's Creed Destiny, that still may be the case. MP1st published a video showing off gameplay and placeholder footage of the allegedly scrapped Assassin's Creed game, which was reportedly being developed by Ubisoft and Tencent.
The video showed off the game's title, but also the 206 BCE setting during the Qin Empire in Ancient China. The gameplay footage shows the playable character scaling castle walls and performing stealth kills in typical Assassin's Creed fashion, while the placeholder videos offer a look at different combat skills and weapons, including a unique option that can only be described as a deadly umbrella.
With this Assassin's Creed game reportedly canceled, we may never see any of this footage make it out of the development graveyard. However, Ubisoft is still working on Assassin's Creed Jade, which was announced in 2022 as a mobile entry in the franchise that's set in ancient China. It's been several years since Ubisoft has revealed anything further about the project, but a 2024 Reuters report said it would be delayed until 2025. The developer still hasn't made any announcements about Assassin's Creed Jade, but a company exec recently told VGC that it would have co-op gameplay. If we're lucky, we might see some of the elements of the reported Assassin's Creed Destiny end up in the upcoming mobile game.

title_en: Android Auto can be used outside of your car: Here's how
title_fa: Android Auto can be used outside of your car: Here's how
excerpt_en: It might sound weird to use Android Auto outside of a vehicle, but doing so has unexpected productivity benefits.
excerpt_fa: It might sound weird to use Android Auto outside of a vehicle, but doing so has unexpected productivity benefits.
content_en:
Android Auto can be used outside of your car: Here's how
A spare tablet, USB cable and $4 app can bring Android Auto to your desk or kitchen counter.
My old Samsung Galaxy Tab had poor battery life, but still had enough juice to be a Google Home control panel. Then I came across an unusual use for it: Android Auto. Yes, the software intended for car dashboards can be used elsewhere with the right app.
Android Auto runs on your phone and projects a simplified interface for maps, music and messaging onto a compatible car display. If you instead install a third-party receiver app on a tablet, it can act as the "car's screen" without a vehicle in sight. And because your phone does the processing, it's great for an aging tablet that has trouble running apps.
With this, it's possible to repurpose an old Android tablet as an Android Auto display in your car. But the same hack can be used on a desk or kitchen counter, where keeping a screen in view may help prevent you from picking up your phone every five minutes. Just don't mistake it for an official Google Home dashboard mode.
How to use Android Auto without a car
For a wired setup, you'll need an Android phone running Android 11 or newer, a spare Android tablet or phone and a data-capable USB cable. Android Auto is already integrated into compatible phones, so you just need to install a receiver app on the second device.
One of them is Open Headunit (formerly Headunit Revived), available for $3.99 on Google Play. It's compatible with Android 5.0 or newer on the receiving device, so older tablets may be worth a shot. However, you'll still need a compatible USB connection, which not all older tablets will play nice with. Another option is Headunit Reloaded, which costs $4.99.
Install Open Headunit on the tablet, then:
- Connect the tablet to your phone using a USB cable (and an OTG adapter if necessary).
- Select Android Auto in your phone's USB options, if prompted.
- Open the app on the tablet, tap USB, grant permission and choose your phone from the device list. Approve any remaining connection prompts on your phone.
Android Auto should then appear on the tablet. If you'd rather avoid keeping your phone connected, both apps also offer Self-Mode, which runs Android Auto on the same device. However, this requires the device to have a working Android Auto installation of its own, which isn't guaranteed on older tablets.
Open Headunit's developer says Android Auto 17.4 and later may require starting the head unit server through Android Auto's developer settings before Self-Mode works. Wireless connections between the two devices are possible, but take more setup. While USB is easier, it occupies the tablet's charging port, which is a problem when the battery is already worn-out.
What's the point when your phone is right there?
Android Auto's driving-friendly design is also a distraction filter. With big controls, you can pause Spotify or skip a podcast without unlocking your phone. Plus, your messages can be read aloud and answered by voice. On compatible systems, Gemini can respond to queries and even manage smart home gadgets via Google Home, although this is not always reliable.
You also don't have your usual parade of apps in front of you. Android Auto only works with a limited selection of apps, so you won't get sucked into spending half an hour on Instagram when you just wanted to check a song title. A spare tablet can sit next to a monitor or on a kitchen stand, doing a few tasks well without constantly needing your attention.
There are compromises, though. If all you want is Spotify or Google Home, running those apps directly on the tablet is simpler. The dashboard can be dominated by maps when you aren't on the move, and it won't be running your normal tablet apps when connected to Android Auto. Anyone in the vicinity may be able to see message notifications.
With both USB and wireless projection, your primary phone has to remain connected, and paid services like Spotify Premium still require their own subscriptions. Google's official setup instructions don't cover using Android Auto on a tablet at home. It's a fun novelty, but expect some quirks.

title_en: What's actually eating all the storage space on your Android Phone?
title_fa: What's actually eating all the storage space on your Android Phone?
excerpt_en: Android phone running out of space? Here's why and what you can do to get rid of old files.
excerpt_fa: Android phone running out of space? Here's why and what you can do to get rid of old files.
content_en:
What's actually eating all the storage space on your Android Phone?
And how you can efficiently delete them to claw back storage on your device.
So, you're running out of storage on your Android phone. It happens, even if you periodically delete files and photos, especially if you've been porting your data from one phone to the next over the past few years. Apps, images, videos and big files you've downloaded and forgotten typically eat up most of your storage space, but there may be some files you don't even know are on your phone. We'll discuss how you can find them and delete them quickly and efficiently.
Apps
One of the most effective ways to free up space is, of course, to uninstall apps. To get an overview of all your apps and to make it easier to decide which ones to delete, go to Settings > Device Care > Storage > Apps. From there, you can see which applications are taking up the most space. Just tap on the app you want to remove and then hit Uninstall.
That said, you can can also just archive apps. Go through the same steps above, and instead of tapping Uninstall, tap Archive instead. Doing so deletes its core software files and temporary data from your phone but retains your login info and personal settings, so you can easily start using the app again after redownloading it.
Android has a feature called "auto-archive," which can automatically archive apps your rarely use when you run low on storage. If you try to install an app on a phone that has no more space, you'll see a pop-up window telling you about auto-archive and giving you the option to switch it on from there. You can also activate the feature anytime you want by going to the Play Storage and tapping on your profile photo at the top right corner. From there, go to Settings > General and then toggle on Automatically archive apps. Google says auto-archiving can free up "nearly 60 percent of an app's storage space, without removing the app presence or users' data from the device."
Images and videos
If you don't care about backing up the media saved on your phone, you can go ahead and delete them all or manually select what you want to get rid of. You can do that in your phone's gallery, or by going to Storage in Settings > Images or Videos and selecting the files you want to remove. But if you want to preserve those memories, the easiest way to do that is to use Google Photos. The app can save cloud backups of your images and videos to your Google account.
All Google accounts come with up to 15GB of free cloud storage, shared across Photos, Drive, Gmail and the company's other services. Since that is, admittedly, tiny and might not be able to accommodate years' worth of images and videos, you may have to pay for a Google One subscription. Google One costs $2 a month for 100GB of storage or $3 a month for 200GB.
Once your images and videos are backed up on the cloud, you can tidy up your phone. In the Photos app, tap on your profile image and go to Free up space on this device. It will delete the items already backed up on the cloud in the quality you choose. You won't see those images in your other gallery apps anymore, but you can still view them in Google Photos.
You can also switch on Smart Storage to automatically clear up images that have already been backed up if it's available on your device. Go to your device Settings > Storage > Free up space. Then, tap the hamburger menu, find Settings from the options you see and switch on Smart Storage.
Other data
But what about the other stuff occupying your storage space, the ones that aren't as obvious as apps and images? Head over to Settings > Device Care > Storage again. You'll a section that says Duplicate files and another that says Large files. Tap on them to see a selection of files you can choose and delete. Scroll down, and you might see more suggestions on what to remove, such as old media files, old downloads, pre-edit image backups and app caches. Tap on each one to review the files you can dispose. You can also view your Storage details and tap on Other files to delete stuff you may have forgotten you had.
If you have streaming and social media apps, don't underestimate what a cache clearing can do. It could free up gigabytes of storage. You should also make it a habit to empty your trash. Go to Settings > Device Care > Storage and find the Trash or the Recycle bin folder to empty out.
